name: Setanta and the hound of Culann: the boy who becomes Cu Chulainn
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The origin scene of the Ulster Cycle's greatest hero, from the Macgnimrada Con Culaind ('The Boyhood Deeds of Cu Chulainn') embedded in the Tain Bo Cuailnge (Recension I, Lebor na hUidre, 12th c. compilation of 7th-9th c. material). T1: the boy's given name is SETANTA -- he is the son of the god LUGH (Lugh Lamhfhada, 'Long-Arm') and the mortal DEICHTINE, sister of King CONCHOBAR MAC NESSA of Ulster; born and raised at DUN DEALGAN (Dundalk), he is a nephew of the king. T2: while the men of Ulster are at a feast at the house of the smith CULANN, Setanta comes late along the road, alone; Conchobar has forgotten to warn Culann that another guest is on the way, and Culann has already loosed his SAVAGE GUARD-HOUND, an enormous chained war-dog kept to protect the smith's forge and cattle. T3: the hound charges Setanta at the gate. The boy has only a HURLING BALL and hurling-stick (the game of iomain that Ulster boys played). He DRIVES THE HURLING BALL DOWN THE HOUND'S THROAT with such force that the ball goes through and out the back of the dog; then he seizes it by the hind legs and dashes its head against a standing stone (Recension I, folio-line 800-830). T4: Culann laments -- the hound was his living defence, and no dog can be bred to match it in less than a year. Setanta, still a boy, kneels and offers to GUARD THE SMITH'S HOUSE HIMSELF in the hound's place until a new pup of the same stock can be trained. The druid CATHBAD, watching, pronounces the new name: from that hour the boy is CU CHULAINN -- 'THE HOUND OF CULANN'. T5: on the SAME DAY Cathbad prophesies that whoever takes up arms for the first time on that date will have SHORT LIFE BUT LASTING FAME. Cu Chulainn, hearing this, RUSHES to arm himself; his adult career and his early death are both sealed in this single boyhood day. The chained hound, the hurling ball, the offer to stand as replacement, the new name, and the fatal prophecy are all one continuous scene in the manuscript. Further rungs: the Macgnimrada is a set of INSET tales that Ferghus mac Roich narrates to Medb inside the Tain, explaining who this boy is who is stopping her army; the 'hurling ball down the throat' is the earliest surviving heroic-child scene in Irish literature; Setanta's paternity is DOUBLE (Deichtine also has a mortal husband Sualtaim mac Roich, so Cu Chulainn is called son of BOTH Lugh and Sualtaim -- typical Celtic 'divine + mortal' parentage).
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, edited and translated by Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976) -- the Macgnimrada Con Culaind inset, folio-lines c.400-1000 covering the birth of Setanta, the hurling-ball hound scene at Culann's house, the naming by Cathbad, and the same-day arms-taking prophecy. Lebor na hUidre ('Book of the Dun Cow', c.1106) and Yellow Book of Lecan (c.1391) as the two manuscript witnesses of Recension I. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969) -- literary translation. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cu Chulainn' and 'Setanta' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Cu Chulainn', 'Culann', 'Cathbad', 'Macgnimrada Con Culaind' -- Setanta's parentage (Lugh + Deichtine), the hurling ball down the hound's throat, the naming by Cathbad, the same-day arms-prophecy of short life and lasting fame. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Recension I says Setanta drives the ball THROUGH the hound (through-and-out) or into the throat only (both readings attested).
framing_note: THE FOUNDATIONAL Cu Chulainn ladder -- every downstream Ulster Cycle topic (Ferdiad, the geasa, the ristrad, the death by the standing stone) leans on the T1/T2 anchor established here (§16 teach-before-test). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (he drives a HURLING BALL DOWN THE THROAT of a war-dog with a stick, then dashes its head on a stone) and T5 (Cathbad prophesies SHORT LIFE + LASTING FAME on the very day he takes up arms). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the boy who killed the guard-hound of Culann' AND ask what he was renamed; describe the SCENE (a boy walking alone up a road with a hurling stick, a savage chained hound loosed at a smith's gate, a hurling ball) and let the recall be the BOY, the NEW NAME, or the OBJECT (the hurling ball). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the boy David killing Goliath with a sling-stone (Christian pillar), the boy Herakles strangling the serpents in his cradle (Greek pillar), or the boy Sigurd taming Grani (Norse pillar) -- a heroic-child scene that names the whole future. Do NOT use 'destined by fate to' framing; use 'that same day the druid said, and the boy did'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other heroic-child kills (David + Goliath -- Christian; Herakles + the serpents -- Greek; Perseus's first monster -- Greek; Sigurd + Fafnir -- Norse), other boyhood-name changes (Sauron/Ann atar in silly modern -- do not use; Jacob renamed Israel -- Christian pillar), other Cuchulainn-adjacent (Fionn's boyhood is a SEPARATE ladder -- do not conflate). Wrong weapon: HURLING BALL AND STICK (iomain equipment), not a spear or sword; his adult weapons come later. Wrong hound-owner: CULANN THE SMITH, not King Conchobar. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: Cu Chulainn is a LEGENDARY figure of Irish pseudo-history; the Tain is a 7th-11th-century literary compilation. State honestly.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the actual Iron Age Ulster kingdom (Emain Macha / Navan Fort, near Armagh, has real 1st-c. BC ceremonial-site archaeology). Theology owns the STORY of the boy Setanta at Culann's gate. GEOGRAPHY owns Dun Dealgan (Dundalk) as a place; theology owns the boyhood-deed that happened there in the legend.

name: The ristrad: Cu Chulainn's warp-spasm
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: Cu Chulainn's monstrous battle-frenzy, from the Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, in the passage where he first attacks Medb's army alone at the ford. T1: RISTRAD (or riastradh, 'the warp-spasm' or 'distortion') is the name for the terrifying battle-transformation that comes over CU CHULAINN when he loses himself in combat; his body reshapes into something no longer human. T2: the Tain describes the ristrad in astonishing physical detail. HIS BODY QUAKES AND SPINS INSIDE ITS SKIN so that his feet and knees swing round to the back and his heels and calves to the front; his HAIR STANDS ON END, each hair sharp as a HAWTHORN THORN with a spark of fire at its tip; ONE EYE SINKS BACK INTO HIS SKULL SO DEEP that a heron could not pluck it out, while the OTHER BULGES OUT ONTO HIS CHEEK as huge as a cauldron. T3: from his mouth a MOUTHFUL OF FIRE goes forth; foam BOILS from between his teeth; the beat of his heart is like the roaring of a lion coming among bears. Above the crown of his head rises the LON LAITH -- the 'HERO-LIGHT' -- a straight jet of dark blood or a column of black smoke, taller than the mast of a ship, that marks him at any distance on the battlefield. T4: in this state he cannot tell friend from foe; when he first returns from his boyhood raid on Nechtain Scene's sons the whole army of Emain Macha are afraid to let him inside the walls. Conchobar's queen MUGAIN sends OUT THREE VATS OF COLD WATER and 150 WOMEN OF EMAIN NAKED to the plain; the sight cools the ristrad off him. He hides his face for shame; they put him in the first vat -- the water BOILS AND BURSTS the staves. Second vat: the water simply boils. Third vat: the water is only made hot as bath-heat, and the boy is himself again (Tain Recension I, boyhood-deeds inset). T5: the ristrad is the SIGNATURE MYTHIC IMAGE of Irish heroic literature -- no Greek hero, no Norse berserker, has anything quite like this: not a mere rage but a physical MELTING of the body into a fighting-shape. It is what makes Cu Chulainn UNBEATABLE in single combat and INCOMPATIBLE with normal society -- three vats of women and cold water are the only known cure. Further rungs: the manuscript description is one of the longest single sustained passages in the Tain; scholars compare it to the Norse berserkergangr (going berserk) but the ristrad is more monstrous and more visual; the LON LAITH ('warrior's moon' or 'hero-light') is the single most iconic single detail -- a black column above the head visible from miles.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, edited by Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976), lines c.2245-2340 for the full ristrad description at the ford, and the boyhood-deeds inset for the three-vat cooling scene. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969) -- English literary translation of the ristrad passage. Ciaran Carson, The Tain (Penguin, 2007). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cu Chulainn' and 'Riastrad' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Cu Chulainn', 'Riastrad', 'Tain Bo Cuailnge' -- the eye swap, hair standing sharp as hawthorn, hero-light lon laith above the skull, the three-vats-of-cold-water cooling scene with the 150 naked women of Emain. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: alternate spellings 'riastrad', 'ristrad', 'riastradh' -- pick one and use consistently.
framing_note: The SIGNATURE MYTHIC-IMAGE ladder -- this is the physical picture Irish literature holds in the world's imagination. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (his feet turn to the back, ONE EYE SINKS IN + THE OTHER BULGES to cheek-size) and T4 (Ulster's women come out NAKED with three vats of water to cool him and the first two vats burst / boil). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe a warrior whose eyes swap and hair stands on fire AND ask what the state is called; describe the SCENE (a warrior at a ford, hair sharp as hawthorn with sparks, a column of dark hero-light rising from the crown) and let the recall be the NAME (ristrad), the LIGHT (lon laith), or the COOLING (the three vats). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same dark weight as the Norse berserkergangr (Norse pillar -- the shirt-shedding fury of Odin's chosen) or Achilles's rage after Patroclus (Greek pillar -- 'as when a hero's eyes glow like coals'). Grade-10 kids can handle the body-horror; Norse and Irish myth are LOUD. Do NOT sanitise; the Tain does not sanitise. DISTRACTOR MINE: other battle-frenzies (Norse BERSERKERGANGR, Greek LYSSA the war-madness personified, biblical GIBBORIM war-fury -- all adjacent-real), other Cu Chulainn features (the Gae Bolg, the geasa -- those are separate ladders), other hero-lights (Moses's face shining from Sinai is DIFFERENT -- Christian pillar). Wrong body-part swap: FEET AND KNEES to the back, one EYE in / one EYE out; not head-spin, not neck-swap.
history_overlap: None with history -- the ristrad is a literary description with no historical anchor. GEOGRAPHY owns Emain Macha (Navan Fort) as a real Ulster site; theology owns the story of the three vats there.

name: Scathach and the Isle of Shadow: Cu Chulainn's training in warcraft
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: Cu Chulainn's apprenticeship to the warrior-woman Scathach, from Tochmarc Emire ('The Wooing of Emer', 8th-9th c., preserved in the Rawlinson B 512 manuscript). T1: SCATHACH ('the Shadowy One') is a legendary WARRIOR-WOMAN who runs a martial school on the ISLE OF SHADOW -- Dun Scaith on the coast of ALBA (Scotland), traditionally identified with the Isle of Skye. She is the greatest teacher of arms in the world of the Ulster Cycle. T2: Cu Chulainn goes to her to complete his training and to earn the right to marry EMER of the fair hair, daughter of Forgall Manach -- Forgall has set the impossible bride-price that his daughter's suitor must first study with Scathach. Cu Chulainn crosses the sea, then the terrifying PLAIN OF ILL-LUCK (Mag nDolor) that eats the unwary, then the PERILOUS GLEN full of ravening beasts, and finally the BRIDGE OF THE CLIFF -- a bridge whose middle rises up when someone tries to walk it and pitches them off; Cu Chulainn crosses only by the SALMON-LEAP, hurling himself from one end to the other. T3: Scathach's own daughter UATHACH lets him in; he trains with Scathach for a year and a day, learning her full arsenal -- among them the SALMON-LEAP (already used at the bridge), the APPLE-FEAT (throwing and catching), the FEATS OF THE SWORD-EDGE and THE ROPE-FEAT, the chariot-feats, and the war-cry that stuns armies. T4: at the same school he meets FERDIAD MAC DAMAN, Scathach's other star pupil, and they become inseparable FOSTER-BROTHERS in arms; they eat from the same dish and sleep with their shields interlocked. Cu Chulainn also joins Scathach in her war against the rival warrior-queen AIFE, defeats Aife in single combat, spares her, and fathers a son on her -- CONNLA -- whom he will one day meet and kill without knowing. T5: as her parting gift Scathach gives Cu Chulainn the GAE BOLG -- the 'belly-spear' or 'notched spear', a weapon so terrible she teaches it to no other pupil. She also prophesies his short life and lasting fame, echoing Cathbad's boyhood prophecy. Everything Cu Chulainn will do at the Ford -- kill Ferdiad, wield the Gae Bolg, endure the ristrad -- traces back to this year and a day on the Isle of Shadow. Further rungs: Scathach is one of the great WARRIOR-WOMEN of world mythology, on the same plane as the Amazon queens or the Valkyries but a TEACHER rather than a fighter alongside; the SALMON-LEAP (leim in bratain) is her signature technique and becomes Cu Chulainn's trademark move at Ferdiad's ford; the Isle of Shadow is traditionally identified with Skye (an Sgitheanach in Scots Gaelic supposedly derives from her name).
source: PRIMARY: Tochmarc Emire ('The Wooing of Emer'), 8th-9th c., preserved in Rawlinson B 512 and other manuscripts, translated by Kuno Meyer (Archaeological Review 1888). Foglaim Con Culainn ('The Training of Cu Chulainn'), later Middle Irish tale. Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, the Comrac Fir Diad ('Combat with Ferdiad') episode for the Gae Bolg backstory. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Scathach' and 'Cu Chulainn' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Scathach', 'Aife', 'Tochmarc Emire', 'Salmon leap' -- Scathach as warrior-woman on Dun Scaith / Isle of Skye, Plain of Ill-Luck + Perilous Glen + Bridge of the Cliff, salmon-leap technique, Ferdiad as fellow pupil, Aife defeated + Connla conceived, Gae Bolg as parting gift. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Scathach or Uathach names the fee for the Gae Bolg training (sources vary).
framing_note: The MENTOR-ARCHETYPE ladder for Cu Chulainn -- Scathach is behind every fighting technique the hero will use. Dinner-test payoffs: T1 (the greatest MARTIAL TEACHER in the Ulster Cycle world is a WOMAN on a Scottish island) and T5 (she gives him the GAE BOLG as a parting gift, a weapon she teaches to NO OTHER pupil). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the woman who trained Cu Chulainn' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a fortress on the Isle of Shadow, a Bridge of the Cliff that pitches walkers off, a year-and-a-day of training) and let the recall be the TEACHER (Scathach), the ISLAND (Isle of Shadow / Skye / Dun Scaith), the FELLOW PUPIL (Ferdiad), or the PARTING WEAPON (Gae Bolg). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Chiron the centaur teaching Achilles (Greek pillar), Merlin arranging Arthur's boyhood (Arthurian pillar), or Elijah training Elisha (Christian pillar) -- an old master shaping a peerless pupil. Scathach as WOMAN teacher is remarkable -- honour it as the myth does. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Cu Chulainn teachers (Cathbad the druid is a PROPHET not a martial teacher, but adjacent-real; Fergus mac Roich his foster-father in Ulster is an EARLIER teacher), other warrior-women (Aife her rival is real in the same story, Boudicca is HISTORY, the Amazons are Greek pillar, the Valkyries are Norse pillar), other legendary schools (Cheiron's cave on Pelion -- Greek). Wrong location: DUN SCAITH on the ISLE OF SHADOW (traditionally Skye in Scotland), not Ireland. Wrong pupil-list: FERDIAD, not Fionn (Fionn is a different cycle).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Isle of Skye (an Sgitheanach) as a real Scottish island; theology owns the LEGEND that Scathach's fortress stood there.

name: The Gae Bolg: the belly-spear cast with the foot
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: Cu Chulainn's signature weapon, from Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I (the Comrac Fir Diad episode) and Tochmarc Emire. T1: the GAE BOLG (Old Irish 'ga bulga', usually translated 'the belly-spear' or 'notched spear') is CU CHULAINN'S SIGNATURE WEAPON -- a spear given to him by SCATHACH on the Isle of Shadow, and the weapon that ends every one of his hardest single combats. T2: the Gae Bolg is not thrown from the hand. It is CAST FROM THE FOOT while the caster STANDS IN THE WATER -- specifically at a ford, in mid-current, kicking the spear across the surface with the toes of the right foot. This method of casting is the only method Scathach ever teaches for it. T3: what makes the Gae Bolg horrible is not the throw but what it does inside the wound. Once the tip enters the enemy's body, it OPENS OUT INTO THIRTY BARBS or 'thirty points' inside the flesh, filling every limb and joint of the target from within (Tain Recension I, Comrac Fir Diad). It cannot be pulled back out -- the wounded man's flesh has to be CUT OPEN to remove the spear, killing him a second time. T4: Cu Chulainn uses the Gae Bolg only in the last extremity. At the FORD in the fight with FERDIAD -- Cu Chulainn's foster-brother from Scathach's school, forced by Queen Medb to fight him -- on the fourth day of combat, when Ferdiad has beaten every ordinary weapon and Cu Chulainn is losing, he calls to his charioteer LOEG for the Gae Bolg. Loeg floats it downstream; Cu Chulainn catches it BETWEEN THE TOES of his right foot and kicks it up under Ferdiad's shield-rim into his belly. T5: as Ferdiad dies Cu Chulainn LIFTS HIM in his arms across the ford so that no Connacht man can spoil his body, and LAMENTS OVER HIM in a long formal lament -- 'Beloved Ferdiad, dear was thy fair form, dear thy grey eye...' -- because Scathach's rule of fosterage bound them together and the queen's war has forced him to kill his own brother-in-arms. The Gae Bolg wins the fight and loses him a brother in the same cast. Further rungs: 'bolg' is glossed variously as 'bag' (a bag-full of barbs), 'notch', 'lightning-flash' or 'belly' -- Old Irish scholarship still debates the etymology; the weapon may originally have been a HARPOON (some scholars link the foot-throw and water-cast to spear-fishing technique); the Gae Bolg is UNIQUE in Irish literature -- no other hero, no other cycle, has anything like it.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, edited by Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976) -- the Comrac Fir Diad (Combat with Ferdiad) episode, lines c.3200-3540 covering the four days of combat, the calling for the Gae Bolg, the foot-cast at the ford, the thirty barbs, and the lament over Ferdiad. Tochmarc Emire, translated by Kuno Meyer (1888) -- Scathach's teaching of the Gae Bolg. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Gae Bolg' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Gae Bolg', 'Cu Chulainn', 'Ferdiad', 'Tain Bo Cuailnge' -- the foot-throw from the water, thirty barbs opening inside the wound, must be cut out with the flesh, given by Scathach, used to kill Ferdiad. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact number of barbs (Recension I says 'thirty', some later versions say 'twenty-four' or 'thirty barbs like a hedgehog').
framing_note: The SIGNATURE-WEAPON ladder -- the Gae Bolg is Irish myth's most famous object. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (it is CAST FROM THE FOOT while STANDING IN WATER, not thrown from the hand) and T3 (once inside the body it OPENS INTO THIRTY BARBS and cannot be removed without cutting the flesh open). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Cu Chulainn's spear that opened into barbs' AND ask what it was called; describe the SCENE (a warrior in mid-ford, charioteer floating a spear down the current, a right foot catching it and kicking it home) and let the recall be the WEAPON (Gae Bolg), the CASTING METHOD (foot-throw), the GIVER (Scathach), or the VICTIM (Ferdiad). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Achilles's spear from Chiron (Greek pillar), Odin's Gungnir made by the sons of Ivaldi (Norse pillar), or Roland's sword Durendal with its holy relics (Western-medieval pillar) -- a hero's named weapon with a named origin and a specific property. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish weapons (Lugh's spear Areadbhar / the Sleg the-spear-that-never-missed of the Tuatha De Danann, Fionn's spear Birgha -- adjacent-real from the Irish tradition), other barbed / uncleanly-removed weapons (Philoctetes's arrow -- Greek; Beowulf's giant-sword that melts -- Norse pillar), other foot-cast weapons (there is essentially none -- this is what makes the Gae Bolg unique). Wrong caster method: FOOT, not hand; from the WATER, not from dry ground. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: the Gae Bolg is pure literary invention -- state honestly.
history_overlap: None with history -- the Gae Bolg is a purely literary weapon.

name: Loeg mac Riangabra and the Grey of Macha: the charioteer and the horses
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: Cu Chulainn's inseparable charioteer and his two named horses, from the Tain Bo Cuailnge and the Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn', in Recension II and the later Book of Leinster tradition). T1: LOEG MAC RIANGABRA is Cu Chulainn's CHARIOTEER -- the man who drives him into every battle, holds the reins in single combat, floats the Gae Bolg down the ford when it is called for, and stays at his lord's shoulder from boyhood to death. In an Ulster Cycle chariot, the driver's role is nearly equal to the warrior's; the two are a fighting pair. T2: Cu Chulainn's two horses have names of their own. THE GREY OF MACHA (Liath Macha, 'grey of Macha') and THE BLACK OF SAINGLIU (Dub Sainglenn, 'black of the Glen of Sainglenn') are said to have risen out of two grey and dark lakes at the moment Cu Chulainn first took up arms; they were caught and tamed by the boy hero and no one else could handle them. T3: the two horses are more than beasts -- they understand what is coming. On the DAY OF CU CHULAINN'S DEATH, when the charioteer Loeg goes to yoke the chariot, the GREY OF MACHA WILL NOT LET HIMSELF BE HARNESSED -- turns his left side three times against Loeg, weeps TEARS OF BLOOD onto Cu Chulainn's feet as the harness is finally put on. This is the omen. T4: at the fatal battle Loeg is killed FIRST by a spear cast by LUGAID -- the same spear that will kill Cu Chulainn is first cast at the charioteer and passes through him. Then the GREY OF MACHA is speared and mortally wounded, and gallops off to a lake weeping to die; the Black of Saingliu also dies. Only after his driver and both horses are dead does Cu Chulainn take his own death-wound. T5: at the very end, when Cu Chulainn is dead upon the standing stone (see the Death ladder), the GREY OF MACHA returns wounded to his master's body. Half-mad with grief, the horse KICKS AND BITES the enemies who come to loot the corpse -- fifty men, the sagas say, are killed by the horse alone before the Grey himself falls. It is the horse, not any man, that avenges the hero. Further rungs: MACHA is the same goddess whose CURSE laid the Ulstermen low (see the Curse of Macha ladder) -- the horse's name binds Cu Chulainn to her; the CHARIOT-CULTURE of the Ulster Cycle has real Iron Age Celtic archaeological anchors (Iron Age chariot burials found in Yorkshire, ceremonial-chariot fittings from Ulster); Loeg's role is one of the fullest portraits of a heroic sidekick in world literature, on the plane of Patroclus with Achilles.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I (O'Rahilly ed.) -- Loeg as constant charioteer, the two horses named at first-arming. Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn'), Book of Leinster and later manuscript tradition, translated in Whitley Stokes (Revue Celtique 1877) and Kinsella (The Tain, 1969) -- the Grey refusing to be harnessed, tears of blood, Loeg killed first by Lugaid's spear, the Grey's revenge on his master's corpse. Serglige Con Culainn ('The Wasting-Sickness of Cu Chulainn') for further Loeg scenes. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cu Chulainn' and 'Liath Macha' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Cu Chulainn', 'Liath Macha', 'Loeg', 'Death of Cu Chulainn' -- Loeg mac Riangabra, Grey of Macha + Black of Saingliu rising from lakes, omens on the death-day, tears of blood, horse killing avengers. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the exact spelling 'Loeg' vs 'Laeg' (Middle Irish forms differ).
framing_note: The COMPANIONS ladder. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (the Grey WEEPS TEARS OF BLOOD on Cu Chulainn's feet as the harness is put on) and T5 (after Cu Chulainn is dead, the wounded HORSE fights on and kills fifty enemies himself). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe a charioteer floating a spear down the ford AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a chariot pair on a battlefield, a warrior and a driver, two horses risen from two lakes) and let the recall be the DRIVER (Loeg), the GREY HORSE (Liath Macha / Grey of Macha), or the BLACK HORSE (Dub Sainglenn / Black of Saingliu). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Patroclus and Achilles (Greek pillar -- the warrior's inseparable second), Sleipnir the eight-legged horse of Odin (Norse pillar -- named heroic mount), or Argus the loyal dog of Odysseus (Greek pillar -- the beast that recognises its master). DISTRACTOR MINE: other charioteers (Krishna as charioteer of Arjuna is OUT-OF-BANK Hindu -- do not use; Automedon as charioteer of Achilles -- Greek pillar, adjacent-real), other legendary horses (Sleipnir -- Norse; Pegasus + Bellerophon -- Greek; Bucephalus + Alexander -- history), other Ulster pairs (Cu Chulainn + Ferdiad is fosterage not chariot-pair). Wrong horse-name: GREY OF MACHA (not Grey of Ulster), BLACK OF SAINGLIU (not Black of Erin).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns real Iron Age Celtic chariot archaeology (Wetwang chariot burial, Yorkshire; Ulster horse-fittings). Theology owns the STORY of Loeg and the two lake-horses.

name: The geasa of Cu Chulainn: taboos that seal a doom
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The taboos laid on Cu Chulainn from birth and the day he breaks them all, from the Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn', Book of Leinster and later versions) and passages scattered through the Ulster Cycle. T1: a GEIS (plural GEASA, pronounced roughly 'gaysh' / 'gaysha') is a magical PROHIBITION laid on a person at birth or by a druid -- an act a hero MUST NEVER DO. In the Ulster Cycle a hero's geasa are placed by druids or fated at birth; every hero has his own set, individually chosen, and breaking one is DEATH. T2: Cu Chulainn's two chief geasa are two-fold and mutually contradictory. FIRST: he MUST NEVER REFUSE FOOD OFFERED TO HIM AT A HEARTH -- to refuse hospitality is unthinkable for a warrior. SECOND: he MUST NEVER EAT THE FLESH OF A DOG -- because he is CU CHULAINN, 'the Hound of Culann', to eat dog-meat is to eat his own name, his own totem, himself. T3: on the day of his death Cu Chulainn is riding out to meet the war-band gathered by the sons of the men he has killed (Erc, Lugaid, and the children of Cailitin). Along the road he passes THREE OLD HAGS -- the daughters of Cailitin, working magic against him -- roasting a DOG on rowan-spits over a fire. They call out and INVITE him to share their meal. T4: Cu Chulainn faces the impossible geasa-trap: to refuse breaks the hospitality-geis; to accept breaks the dog-flesh-geis. Compelled by the hospitality-geis he takes a piece of the roast dog with his LEFT HAND. In the same instant his LEFT HAND WITHERS from shoulder to fingertip -- his sword-arm and shield-arm on that side both go dead. He rides on to the battle already broken. T5: this deliberate SETTING of the geasa AGAINST EACH OTHER is the classic Irish tragic device -- the hero cannot obey both; one geis forces him to violate the other; the trap is airtight, and the hags know it. GEIS is the Ulster Cycle's version of Greek MOIRA (fate) and Norse WYRD (doom) -- but personalised, active, laid on the individual by a druid and enforceable at any moment by anyone clever enough to set the trap. Further rungs: the geasa system runs through ALL of Irish legend -- see Diarmuid's geis to elope with Grainne (Fenian Cycle, a different ladder); Conaire Mor the High King in Togail Bruidne Da Derga ('The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel') dies because ALL his geasa are broken in a single night by a chain of unavoidable acts; the Middle Irish word 'gessa' is cognate with the modern Irish 'geis' still used in Gaeltacht speech.

Togail Bruidne Da Derga ('The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel'), 11th c., for the Conaire Mor geasa-cascade parallel. Tochmarc Emire for boyhood geasa references. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (his two geasa are DELIBERATELY CONTRADICTORY -- never refuse food, never eat dog-flesh, and he's called the HOUND) and T4 (three HAGS roast a DOG on ROWAN SPITS and invite him -- the trap he cannot escape). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the taboos that killed Cu Chulainn' AND ask what they were called; describe the SCENE (three hags at a roadside fire, a roasted dog on spits, a warrior forced to choose between his two vows) and let the recall be the CONCEPT (geis / geasa), the HAGS (daughters of Cailitin), or the BODY-PART that withers (the left hand). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Greek MOIRA that gives Achilles his short-life choice (Greek pillar), Norse WYRD binding Sigurd to his ring (Norse pillar), or the LAW that binds Samson to his hair (Christian pillar) -- a mythic system where one hidden rule can end a hero. Wrong prohibition: the dog-flesh geis is CENTRAL because of the name Cu Chulainn = 'Hound of Culann' -- eating dog is eating his own name.
history_overlap: None with history -- geasa are a literary system.

name: The Cattle Raid of Cooley: Medb, Ailill, and the pillow-talk that started a war
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The framing quarrel that launches the Tain Bo Cuailnge ('The Cattle Raid of Cooley'), from Recension I (O'Rahilly ed.), opening episode 'The Pillow Talk'. T1: the TAIN BO CUAILNGE -- 'The Cattle Raid of Cooley' -- is the CENTRAL EPIC of the Ulster Cycle and the longest single work of medieval Irish literature. Its whole plot is set in motion by a QUARREL BETWEEN A KING AND A QUEEN IN BED. T2: QUEEN MEDB (anglicised Maeve) of CONNACHT and her husband KING AILILL lie in bed at CRUACHAN and begin to compare their wealth. They line up every possession -- their gold, their servants, their weapons, their flocks, their herds -- and the tally is EXACTLY EQUAL, item for item, except for ONE THING. T3: Ailill has ONE BULL -- the great white-horned FINNBENNACH ('the White-Horned') -- that Medb has no equal to. Finnbennach was originally born in Medb's own herd, but the bull refused to be owned by a woman and crossed over to Ailill's herd. Medb has no bull to match him, and it eats at her that Ailill can outshine her by ONE ANIMAL. T4: hearing that the only bull in Ireland who can match Finnbennach is the DONN CUAILNGE -- the great brown BULL OF COOLEY -- kept by a farmer named Daire mac Fiachna in the Cooley peninsula of Ulster, Medb sends messengers to lease him for a year for a fair price. The talks go well until Medb's messengers, drunk at the feast, boast that if Daire had refused they'd have taken the bull by force. Daire hears them, refuses; Medb DECLARES WAR ON ULSTER over one bull. T5: Medb raises an ARMY OF THE FOUR PROVINCES of Ireland (Connacht, Munster, Leinster, and defector Ulstermen under Fergus mac Roich) and marches on Cooley. All of this -- the greatest war in Irish myth, the four days at the Ford, Cu Chulainn's ristrad, the death of Ferdiad, the death of every named champion of Connacht -- follows from ONE HUSBAND-AND-WIFE ARGUMENT ABOUT A BULL in bed. Medb is a WARRIOR-QUEEN in her own right; she rides in her own chariot, kills in single combat, and drives the war herself while Ailill stays largely in her shadow. Further rungs: the OPENING SCENE (the pillow talk) is one of the most famous framing devices in world literature -- an ENTIRE EPIC set off by a domestic argument; MEDB'S NAME ('she who intoxicates') is cognate with English 'mead' and she is closely tied to a sovereignty-goddess archetype -- kings of Connacht traditionally 'married' her at inauguration; the pillow-talk is preserved in full in Recension I on the opening folios, translated word-for-word in Kinsella.
