Book of Leinster Recension II for the fuller version. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969) -- opening chapter 'The Pillow Talk'. Ciaran Carson, The Tain (Penguin, 2007). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Tain Bo Cuailnge' and 'Medb' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Tain Bo Cuailnge', 'Medb', 'Ailill mac Mata', 'Finnbennach', 'Donn Cuailnge' -- the pillow-talk quarrel at Cruachan, Finnbennach the White-Horned refusing to be owned by a woman, the failed lease of the Donn Cuailnge from Daire, drunken boast, war declared. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Recension I says Ailill's bull was ORIGINALLY Medb's (yes -- refused to be owned by a woman is a key detail).
framing_note: The FRAMING-QUARREL ladder -- the opening scene that sets the whole Tain in motion. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (a king and queen in bed COMPARING THEIR WEALTH item by item) and T3 (the Finnbennach bull REFUSED to be owned by a woman and defected to the king's herd, and this is what she cannot bear). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the queen who started a war over a bull' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a bed in Cruachan, wealth compared item by item, one bull the difference, an army raised) and let the recall be the QUEEN (Medb), the KING (Ailill), the BULL (Finnbennach or Donn Cuailnge), or the PLACE (Cruachan). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Helen of Troy launching a thousand ships (Greek pillar) or Guinevere's affair breaking Camelot (Arthurian pillar) -- a domestic-scale grievance that ends a civilisation. Medb is NOT a comic figure; she is a warrior-queen every bit as serious as Odin or Zeus. DISTRACTOR MINE: other war-starters (Helen at Troy -- Greek; Guinevere at Camelot -- Arthurian; Bathsheba and David -- Christian pillar), other Irish queens (Deirdre of the Sorrows also from the Ulster Cycle -- adjacent-real from the same tradition), other queen-vs-king quarrels. Wrong king: AILILL of Connacht, not any Ulster king; Conchobar mac Nessa rules Ulster and is the opponent. Wrong bulls: FINNBENNACH (Ailill's white-horned) and DONN CUAILNGE (the brown bull of Cooley) -- both real named bulls of the Tain, easy to confuse.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Cruachan (Rathcroghan in County Roscommon) as a real Iron Age royal site and Cooley Peninsula as a real place. Theology owns the STORY of the pillow talk and the war for the bull.

name: The Curse of Macha: why the Ulstermen lay in their beds
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The reason Cu Chulainn stands alone at the ford, from Noinden Ulad ('The Debility of the Ulstermen'), 8th-9th c., preserved in the Book of Leinster and other manuscripts. T1: MACHA is a supernatural woman -- variously a goddess of Ulster, one of the three MORRIGAN sisters, or a mortal woman with faery gifts, depending on which version of the story. Emain Macha, the royal seat of Ulster, is named for her (Emain Macha = 'twins of Macha' or 'brooch of Macha' -- both etymologies attested). T2: Macha comes to live secretly with an Ulster farmer named CRUNNIUC and blesses his household with prosperity. One day Crunniuc rides out to the great HORSE FAIR at the assembly of the Ulster king CONCHOBAR MAC NESSA. As the royal horses gallop past he boasts drunkenly that his own wife could OUTRUN THE KING'S HORSES. The boast is reported to the king. T3: Conchobar sends soldiers to fetch Macha and forces her, though she is HEAVILY PREGNANT and NEAR HER TIME, to run against the royal chariot-horses at the assembly. She pleads to be let alone until the child is born -- the assembly refuses. She runs, wins the race by a length, and at the finish line COLLAPSES AND GIVES BIRTH TO TWINS on the ground before them all. T4: in the anguish of childbirth Macha CURSES the men of Ulster. From that hour, in the HOUR OF ULSTER'S GREATEST NEED, every FIGHTING MAN of Ulster shall be laid low with the PANGS OF CHILDBIRTH -- the sharp bed-pain of a woman in labour -- for NINE TIMES NINE DAYS. The curse falls on nine generations of Ulster warriors. T5: this is why when MEDB'S ARMY invades in the Tain and marches on Cooley, the WHOLE FIGHTING FORCE OF ULSTER IS BEDRIDDEN and helpless. Only CU CHULAINN -- because he is a half-god, and because he was NOT BORN in Ulster (or, in some versions, because he is not yet grown -- versions differ) -- is IMMUNE to the curse, and stands ALONE at the fords defending the province single-handed. The whole story of Cu Chulainn's one-man defence of Ulster depends on Macha's curse from an earlier generation. Further rungs: the story is one of the DEEP MYTHIC ORIGINS of Ulster geography (Emain Macha, near modern Armagh, was the real ceremonial capital of the Iron Age Ulaid); the CHILDBIRTH-PAINS-ON-WARRIORS motif is unique in world mythology; Macha is one of THREE MACHAS in Irish tradition -- (1) the wife of Nemed, (2) Macha Mong Ruad the warrior-queen and only High Queen of Ireland, (3) the Macha of the curse -- and medieval scribes sometimes conflate them; Cu Chulainn's own grey horse is named LIATH MACHA ('Grey of Macha') in her honour.
source: PRIMARY: Noinden Ulad ('The Debility of the Ulstermen'), 8th-9th c., preserved in the Book of Leinster (c.1160) and Harleian 5280, translated by Vernam Hull (Celtica 8, 1968) and in Jeffrey Gantz, Early Irish Myths and Sagas (Penguin, 1981). Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I references the curse as the reason for the Ulstermen's incapacity. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Macha' and 'Noinden Ulad' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Macha', 'Emain Macha', 'Noinden Ulad', 'Cu Chulainn' -- Macha marrying Crunniuc, drunken boast, forced footrace against king's horses while pregnant, twins born at the finish, curse of nine-times-nine days of childbirth-pangs. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact duration of the curse (Noinden = 'nine days'; whether it is nine days or nine-times-nine varies by manuscript).
framing_note: The 'WHY IS HE ALONE' ladder -- the mythic setup that makes Cu Chulainn's whole one-man-defence possible. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (a PREGNANT woman is forced to RACE the king's horses and gives birth AT THE FINISH LINE) and T4 (her curse is that the warriors of Ulster will feel WOMEN'S CHILDBIRTH-PAINS in the hour of need). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the curse that laid the Ulstermen in their beds' AND ask who cursed them; describe the SCENE (a pregnant woman forced to outrun a king's chariot, twins born at the finish, a curse called down in labour-pangs) and let the recall be the WOMAN (Macha), the CURSE (childbirth-pains), the KING (Conchobar), or the DURATION (nine-times-nine days). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the CURSE ON THE HOUSE OF ATREUS (Greek pillar -- Agamemnon's line pursued by the Furies), the DOOM OF THE VOLSUNGS (Norse pillar -- Sigurd's ring), or the CURSE OF CAIN (Christian pillar -- a hero-generation marked for suffering). Curse-magic told with full weight, no editorial. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish curses / geasa (Cu Chulainn's own geasa, Diarmuid's elopement-geis -- adjacent), other pregnant-women-of-power (Deirdre of the Sorrows in the same Ulster Cycle is prophesied while in the womb -- adjacent-real), other Macha figures (the wife of Nemed, Macha Mong Ruad the High Queen -- three distinct Machas in Irish tradition, easy to confuse). Wrong duration: the curse comes in bouts of FIVE DAYS AND FOUR NIGHTS every nine generations, not one continuous curse (some retellings simplify).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Emain Macha (Navan Fort near Armagh) as a real Iron Age ceremonial site; theology owns the story of Macha's twins and the curse that named the place.

name: Ferdiad at the Ford: four days killing a foster-brother
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The Comrac Fir Diad ('The Combat with Ferdiad'), the central set-piece of the Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, in which Cu Chulainn kills his fellow pupil and foster-brother. T1: FERDIAD MAC DAMAN is a warrior of Connacht, sworn to Queen MEDB, and a SON OF DAMAN of the Firbolgs. He and CU CHULAINN trained together under SCATHACH on the Isle of Shadow -- they are FOSTER-BROTHERS in arms, having eaten from the same dish, slept under the same shield, and learned the same feats side by side. T2: as Cu Chulainn kills champion after champion at the fords of the Tain, Medb runs out of Connacht warriors willing to face him. She sends for FERDIAD -- the only man in her army who trained under Scathach and knows all the feats. Ferdiad REFUSES; he will not fight his own foster-brother. Medb SHAMES him with satire (the fili's satire being a genuine weapon in the culture -- a poet could blister a warrior's face with public verse), and Ferdiad, unable to bear the shame, accepts. T3: at the ford (later called Ath Fir Diad, 'the Ford of Ferdiad', in County Louth) the two meet on Day One. They fight with CASTING SPEARS all morning and neither can wound the other; that evening they DISMISS THEIR CHARIOTS, EMBRACE, kiss three times, share food from the same store, and both charioteers make one bed for the two of them from their spread cloaks. Day Two: heavier throwing-spears -- they wound each other; end of day, same embrace, same shared bed. Day Three: heavy thrusting-spears -- terrible wounds; end of day the embrace is COLDER, they sleep apart. T4: on the FOURTH DAY, Cu Chulainn calls to LOEG for the GAE BOLG -- the weapon Scathach never taught to Ferdiad. Ferdiad has been raising his shield against ordinary spear-casts all day; the Gae Bolg comes not from the hand but from the FOOT UNDER the shield-rim, kicked from the water. It strikes home. Ferdiad falls. T5: Cu Chulainn LIFTS THE DYING FERDIAD in his arms across the ford to keep his body on the Ulster side, out of reach of Connacht spoilers. He LAMENTS OVER HIM in a long formal lament, keeping vigil beside the corpse: 'Beloved Ferdiad, dear was thy fair form, dear thy grey eye, dear thy wisdom, dear thy speech...' Cu Chulainn is left unable to stand from his wounds; the ford is named for the dead man; Medb's army is one champion poorer and no closer to Cooley. The whole four days is the LONGEST SET-PIECE of the Tain and the emotional heart of the epic. Further rungs: the four-day escalating combat with the shared bed of embrace is UNIQUE in world epic -- no Iliad episode is quite like it; the LAMENT OVER THE DEAD FRIEND parallels Achilles over Patroclus and David over Jonathan; some scholars read a HOMOEROTIC bond into the shared bed and kisses -- others read the pure fosterage-vow of Celtic warrior culture; either way the LOVE between them is the point.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, edited by Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976), Comrac Fir Diad ('The Combat with Ferdiad'), lines c.3200-3600 -- Medb's summons, satire, four days of escalating weapons, shared meals and bed for the first three nights, the Gae Bolg cast, Cu Chulainn's lament. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969) -- 'The Combat of Ferdia and Cuchulain'. Ciaran Carson, The Tain (Penguin, 2007). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Ferdiad' and 'Cu Chulainn' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Ferdiad', 'Comrac Fir Diad', 'Tain Bo Cuailnge' -- fosterage under Scathach, Medb's satire-shaming, four escalating days, kiss and shared bed for three nights, Gae Bolg on day four, lament of Cu Chulainn. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the lament in Kinsella's translation begins 'Ferdiad slain by treachery' or 'Beloved Ferdiad' -- pick the widely-cited line.
framing_note: The GREATEST-COMBAT ladder -- the emotional and dramatic peak of the Tain. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (they FIGHT ALL DAY, then EMBRACE AND SLEEP IN THE SAME BED at night, three nights running) and T4 (Cu Chulainn wins only by using the GAE BOLG -- the weapon Scathach NEVER TAUGHT to Ferdiad -- kicked from the water under the shield). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Cu Chulainn's foster-brother killed at the ford' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (four days of single combat at a river ford, embraces and shared beds at night, a Connacht warrior driven by satire, a spear kicked from the foot) and let the recall be FERDIAD, the FORD (Ath Fir Diad in Louth), the SHAMING (satire by the fili), or the WEAPON (Gae Bolg). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Achilles killing Hector or grieving over Patroclus (Greek pillar), Roland grieving for Oliver at Roncesvalles (Western-medieval pillar), or David lamenting for Jonathan 'thy love to me was wonderful' (Christian pillar) -- warrior-love and warrior-grief. HANDLE the shared-bed / kiss detail with the same weight the Tain does -- neither sanitise nor sensationalise. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Cu Chulainn opponents (the son Connla whom he kills unknowingly is a DIFFERENT tragic-killing ladder; Nadcrantail, Loch mac Emonis -- other Tain ford-opponents, all real), other epic-friend killings (Achilles + Hector, Achilles + Patroclus -- Greek pillar; Beowulf + Grendel is different), other Connacht champions (Fergus mac Roich, Cet mac Magach -- Ulster-Connacht figures). Wrong weapon: GAE BOLG on the fourth day only, kicked from the FOOT in the WATER. Wrong shaming-method: SATIRE by the fili (poet), not open command.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns County Louth (where Ath Fir Diad, the traditional Ford of Ferdiad, is located near modern Ardee -- 'Baile Atha Fhirdhia'); theology owns the STORY of the four days at the ford.

name: The two bulls at the end of the Tain: Donn Cuailnge and Finnbennach
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The final scene of the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the bull-fight that gives the whole war its resolution, from Recension I closing episode. T1: the WHOLE WAR of the Tain has been over ONE THING -- MEDB's need to match her husband AILILL's white bull FINNBENNACH ('the White-Horned') with an equal bull for her own herd. She has spent thousands of lives and destroyed her champion Ferdiad to STEAL THE DONN CUAILNGE, the great BROWN BULL OF COOLEY, from Ulster. T2: even after CU CHULAINN's single-handed defence collapses (when the Ulstermen recover from Macha's curse and rally to the field), Medb has managed one thing -- her men have driven the DONN CUAILNGE off into Connacht. She has her bull. But no one has thought what will happen when two king-bulls meet. T3: back at CRUACHAN in Connacht, the DONN CUAILNGE (Ulster's brown bull) and the FINNBENNACH (Connacht's white-horned) are penned in the same enclosure. When they see each other, they FIGHT. The whole assembly comes out to watch. T4: the two bulls fight ALL DAY AND ALL NIGHT across the length and breadth of Ireland, tearing up the ground with their hooves, bellowing so that no one can sleep. In the morning the DONN CUAILNGE emerges VICTORIOUS, carrying the CORPSE of FINNBENNACH SCATTERED ON HIS HORNS -- a piece of loin here, a piece of shoulder there, dropping BODY-PARTS AT PLACE-NAMES that Ulster still bears (a shin-bone at Ath Luain 'Ford of the Loin', at Trim, and other named landmarks). T5: the Donn Cuailnge then RUNS HOME to Ulster, bellowing madly, dropping the last of Finnbennach's carcass as he goes. When he reaches his own country, he SETS HIS BACK AGAINST A HILL and his HEART BURSTS with fury -- he dies of the exertion, of grief, or of some combination the story leaves unsettled. Both bulls are dead. The whole war has produced NOTHING -- one bull ate the other, then died of the eating, and Medb and Ailill go home with less than they started with. The Tain ends on this bleak note: no victor, no plunder, only exhaustion and dead bulls. Further rungs: the two bulls are REINCARNATED PIGSWAINS from an earlier tale (De Chophur in da Muccida, 'The Quarrel of the Two Pig-Keepers') where two supernatural swineherds turn into different animals through many births and end as these bulls -- the war is only the last stage of a much older enmity; the PLACE-NAMES of Ulster ending in 'Ath' (ford) and 'Sliabh' (hill) are sometimes read in the tale as landing-places of Finnbennach's scattered body-parts, a mythic origin for real geography; the endless-quarrel-over-a-bull is one of world literature's darkest anti-war endings.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, edited by Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976), closing lines -- the bulls penned together at Cruachan, the all-night fight across Ireland, Donn Cuailnge victorious with Finnbennach's carcass on his horns, the scattering of body-parts and place-names, the heart-burst at Ulster. De Chophur in da Muccida ('The Quarrel of the Two Pig-Keepers'), 8th-9th c., for the reincarnation backstory of the two bulls. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969) -- closing chapter. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Tain Bo Cuailnge' and 'Donn Cuailnge' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Donn Cuailnge', 'Finnbennach', 'Tain Bo Cuailnge' -- the two bulls fighting at Cruachan, the all-night combat across Ireland, Finnbennach's carcass on Donn Cuailnge's horns, place-names formed from scattered body-parts, the heart-burst of Donn Cuailnge in Ulster. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: which specific place-names Recension I attaches to which body-parts (spleen at Ath Cliath / Dublin is one commonly cited).
framing_note: The ANTI-CLIMAX ladder -- the war is over a bull and ends with both bulls dead. Dinner-test payoffs: T4 (the winning bull carries the LOSING bull's body-parts SCATTERED ON HIS HORNS as he runs across Ireland, and where each piece falls a PLACE-NAME is born) and T5 (the winning bull then DIES OF ITS OWN FURY, heart bursting against a hill -- BOTH bulls dead, whole war for nothing). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the two bulls whose fight ended the Tain' AND ask their names; describe the SCENE (two king-bulls penned together after a war for one of them, an all-night fight across Ireland, body-parts scattered on a winner's horns) and let the recall be the WINNING BULL (Donn Cuailnge), the LOSING BULL (Finnbennach), or the OUTCOME (both die). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same bleak weight as the ending of the ILIAD (Greek pillar -- Hector buried, Achilles doomed, Troy still standing but everyone knows what comes next) or RAGNAROK (Norse pillar -- gods and giants fall together, world burns and returns) -- an epic that refuses to give victory. DO NOT soften; the Tain ends bleakly. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Tain figures (Medb, Ailill, Cu Chulainn -- from the same story), other legendary Irish cattle (the cows of Bo Finn, the cows of the Milesians), other epic anti-climaxes. Wrong survivor: NEITHER survives; both are dead. Wrong homeland: DONN CUAILNGE from COOLEY in Ulster, FINNBENNACH from Ai in Connacht.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Irish place-names supposedly formed from the scattered body-parts (Ath Luain is now Athlone; several Ulster hills carry legendary names) -- theology owns the STORY that named them.

name: The death of Cu Chulainn: tied standing to Clochafarmore
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The end of Cu Chulainn, from the Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn'), Book of Leinster c.1160 tradition. T1: CU CHULAINN is killed at the age of twenty-seven by a war-band raised against him by the sons of the men he has killed -- LUGAID MAC CON ROI (avenging his father), ERC MAC CAIRPRE (avenging his father Cairbre Nia Fer), and the sorcerous children of CAILITIN (working magic against him from the moment they were born to it). T2: he goes to the fight already broken. He has just broken his three geasa on the same day (see the Geasa ladder) -- the hags of Cailitin trapped him into eating dog-flesh, his LEFT ARM has withered, his LOEG the charioteer has already been killed by a first spear-cast, and his GREY OF MACHA has taken a mortal wound in the fight (see the Loeg ladder). T3: pierced through the belly by LUGAID's spear (the same weapon-shaft that killed Loeg and wounded the Grey), Cu Chulainn stumbles down to the LOUGH nearby to drink and wash his wound. Knowing he cannot stand long and refusing to die on his back, he STRAPS HIMSELF UPRIGHT to a STANDING STONE -- the pillar now called CLOCHAFARMORE, 'the Stone of the Great Man', still standing in a field near Knockbridge in County Louth -- with his own belt or with the strap of his sword, so that he can face his enemies dying on his feet. T4: even mortally wounded and tied to the stone he keeps his sword in hand; his enemies stand off at a distance, afraid to approach the standing corpse. They wait for the sign. On the third day a RAVEN (the MORRIGAN, the war-goddess in bird-form, come at last for him) LANDS ON HIS SHOULDER and drinks the blood at his wound; only then do they know he is truly dead and dare to come close. Lugaid then cuts off the hero's head. T5: this DEATH-STANDING, tied upright to a stone so as never to fall, is the SIGNATURE IMAGE of Cu Chulainn in the world's imagination -- the reason Oliver Sheppard's 1911 bronze statue of THE DYING CUCHULAIN (a naked hero tied to a stone with a raven on his shoulder) stands in Dublin's General Post Office as the memorial of the 1916 Easter Rising. Clochafarmore, the actual stone, still stands in the field where the story places his death, a real granite pillar. The MORRIGAN as raven -- the war-goddess he refused when she offered herself to him in life -- is what confirms his death. Further rungs: Cu Chulainn's SEVERED HEAD in some versions LAUGHS as it falls, terrifying his killers; his SWORD-HAND spasms and takes off the hand of the man cutting his head off (Recension II tradition); the SHEPPARD STATUE in the GPO is deeply tied to Irish national memory; his AGE at death, twenty-seven, is fixed by the two prophecies (Cathbad's boyhood 'short life' and Scathach's later confirmation).
source: PRIMARY: Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn'), Book of Leinster (c.1160) and other manuscripts, translated by Whitley Stokes (Revue Celtique 1877) and in Kinsella (The Tain, 1969, appendix). Also referenced in Serglige Con Culainn and the later Brislech Mor Maige Muirthemni ('The Great Rout on Muirthemne Plain'), 8th-9th c., preserved in Lebor na hUidre and other manuscripts, edited by Bettina Kimpton (2009). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cu Chulainn' and 'Death of Cu Chulainn' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Cu Chulainn', 'Death of Cu Chulainn', 'Clochafarmore', 'Oliver Sheppard' -- Lugaid's spear, standing tied to Clochafarmore, raven on shoulder confirming death, Sheppard's 1911 bronze in the GPO. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the sources say Cu Chulainn ties himself with HIS OWN BELT or with the STRAP OF HIS SWORD (versions vary; both are attested).
framing_note: The DEATH ladder -- the signature death-image of Irish myth. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (he STRAPS HIMSELF STANDING to a stone so he can DIE ON HIS FEET) and T4 (a RAVEN lands on his shoulder to drink his blood and only THEN do his enemies know he is dead). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the hero who tied himself to a stone to die standing' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a mortally wounded warrior at a lake, tying himself upright to a standing stone, a raven landing on his shoulder as the sign) and let the recall be the HERO (Cu Chulainn), the STONE (Clochafarmore in Louth), the BIRD (the raven / the Morrigan), or the KILLER (Lugaid mac Con Roi). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the death of ROLAND at Roncesvalles blowing the Olifant with his last breath (Western-medieval pillar), the death of BEOWULF against the dragon (Norse pillar), or the death of SAMSON pulling the pillars down (Christian pillar) -- a hero refusing to die anything but on his own terms. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Ulster Cycle deaths (Conchobar mac Nessa dies of a brain-ball lodged in his skull from the Battle of Airtech -- adjacent-real from same cycle), other epic deaths (Roland, Beowulf, Samson, Achilles by Paris's arrow -- other pillars), other Cu Chulainn things (the ristrad, the Gae Bolg, the geasa -- separate ladders). Wrong stone: CLOCHAFARMORE ('Stone of the Great Man') in County Louth, a real granite pillar still standing. Wrong killer: LUGAID MAC CON ROI (avenging his father), not Ferdiad (who died at the ford earlier) and not Medb personally. Wrong bird: RAVEN (the Morrigan), not eagle or crow.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the real standing stone CLOCHAFARMORE (near Knockbridge, County Louth) as an archaeological monument; theology owns the STORY of the hero's death against it. HISTORY owns Oliver Sheppard's 1911 bronze in Dublin's GPO and its role in the memory of the 1916 Rising; theology owns the mythic figure the statue depicts.

name: The Champion's Portion at Bricriu's Feast: the beheading game
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: Fled Bricrenn ('Bricriu's Feast'), an Ulster Cycle tale, 8th-9th c. in Lebor na hUidre, closing scene with the giant Uath. T1: BRICRIU MAC CARBADA is a mischief-maker of Ulster -- a poet with a tongue so bitter that Ulster's warriors refuse to sit at his feast unless he can be kept SEPARATE, in a raised gallery, so his poison-verses cannot reach them across the hall. He builds a great hall and invites all Ulster to a feast, whispering privately to THREE separate champions -- CU CHULAINN, CONALL CERNACH, and LOEGAIRE BUADACH -- that each of them will get the CURADMIR, the 'CHAMPION'S PORTION' (the best cut of the roast, given to the greatest warrior). T2: predictably the three champions all demand the portion at once, and Bricriu's plan works -- the hall erupts into a fight. Their wives quarrel too (the 'Women's War of Words'). Every trial ordered to settle it -- combat, judgment by kings, contest at the well -- comes out inconclusive. The three are truly close in prowess. T3: at last a GIANT (called UATH IN THE STRANGER, a shape-shifting bachlach or 'churl' in a form of terrifying size) enters the hall and offers a bargain: 'I WILL LAY MY NECK ON THE BLOCK IF ONE OF YOU WILL DO THE SAME TOMORROW. Strike off my head tonight; take yours in the morning.' T4: LOEGAIRE takes the axe first, cuts off the giant's head with a mighty stroke. The giant STANDS UP, PICKS UP HIS OWN HEAD, tucks it under his arm, and walks out. Next morning he returns, head back on, and offers Loegaire the axe. Loegaire flees. Same next night with CONALL -- Conall beheads the giant, giant walks off with head, comes back, Conall flees. On the third night CU CHULAINN takes the axe, strikes off the giant's head, and next morning WHEN THE GIANT RETURNS Cu Chulainn stretches his neck ON THE BLOCK without flinching. T5: the giant raises the axe -- turns it in his hand -- and STRIKES CU CHULAINN'S NECK WITH THE FLAT (or the back / blunt edge) of the blade, leaving him unharmed. The giant then throws off his disguise (in some versions he is CU ROI MAC DAIRE, the warrior-king of Kerry, come as judge) and pronounces CU CHULAINN THE CHAMPION OF ULSTER by all right: 'You alone kept the bargain.' The tale ends with the Curadmir decided at last. This story -- the BEHEADING GAME with a supernatural stranger who returns to take his own blow -- is the direct ancestor of the medieval English SIR GAWAIN AND THE GREEN KNIGHT (14th c.), which uses the same plot beat-for-beat six centuries later. Further rungs: Fled Bricrenn is the OLDEST attested beheading-game in world literature; the identification of the giant with CU ROI MAC DAIRE, Munster warrior-king, is part of a larger Ulster / Munster rivalry running through the cycle; the SGGK author was almost certainly drawing on Celtic-French intermediaries carrying this material; Bricriu's tongue is so poisonous he tries the same trick multiple times and is himself CRUSHED under a fallen wall in a later tale, which is treated as poetic justice.
source: PRIMARY: Fled Bricrenn ('Bricriu's Feast'), 8th-9th c., preserved in Lebor na hUidre (c.1106) and other manuscripts, edited by George Henderson (Irish Texts Society, 1899). Also translated in Jeffrey Gantz, Early Irish Myths and Sagas (Penguin, 1981). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Fled Bricrenn' and 'Beheading game' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Fled Bricrenn', 'Champion's Portion', 'Cu Roi mac Daire', 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight' -- Bricriu's three-way trick, the Curadmir claim, the giant Uath / Cu Roi's beheading-bargain, Loegaire and Conall fleeing on the return day, Cu Chulainn stretching his neck and receiving the flat of the axe. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the giant strikes with the FLAT of the blade or the BACK (blunt edge) -- Henderson's edition specifies; also confirm the SGGK connection is scholarly consensus.
framing_note: The BEHEADING-GAME ladder -- the tale that seeded Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Dinner-test payoffs: T3+T4 (a giant offers strike-for-strike, gets beheaded, PICKS UP HIS HEAD and walks off, comes back next morning to collect) and T5 (Cu Chulainn is the only one who keeps his half of the bargain, and the giant SPARES him with the flat of the axe). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the hero who stretched his neck on the block and was spared' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a great hall in Ulster, three champions quarrelling over the Curadmir, a giant with an axe offering a bargain, a head walking off under an arm) and let the recall be the HERO (Cu Chulainn), the GAME (the beheading-bargain / Champion's Portion / Curadmir), the FEAST-HOST (Bricriu), or the GIANT (Uath / Cu Roi). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the exchange of blows in SIR GAWAIN AND THE GREEN KNIGHT (Arthurian pillar -- the direct DESCENDANT of this tale) or the trials of the disciples of Sokrates (Greek pillar -- courage under test), but framed as the OLDER of the two -- kids should know Fled Bricrenn is the source. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Ulster champions (Conall Cernach, Loegaire Buadach -- the OTHER TWO who fail this test, both real Ulster warriors), other beheading-game stories (Sir Gawain and the Green Knight -- the direct descendant, adjacent-real from a different pillar; Perceval's various tests -- adjacent), other feast-quarrels (the Judgment of Paris beginning at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis -- Greek pillar). Wrong outcome: Cu Chulainn is the ONE who keeps the bargain; the other two flee. Wrong feast-host: BRICRIU MAC CARBADA, the sharp-tongued poet, not Conchobar.
history_overlap: None with history -- Fled Bricrenn is a literary tale. Cross-pillar overlap: the direct descendant is SIR GAWAIN AND THE GREEN KNIGHT (Arthurian pillar / Middle English 14th c.) -- both are theology-bank material; key on FLED BRICRENN as the ancestor rather than the descendant.

name: Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Salmon of Wisdom
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The origin of Fionn's supernatural knowledge, from the Macgnimartha Finn ('The Boyhood Deeds of Fionn'), Middle Irish, preserved in the Laud 610 manuscript (Bodleian). T1: FIONN MAC CUMHAILL (anglicised 'Finn MacCool') is the great hero of Ireland's FENIAN CYCLE and chief of the FIANNA, the roving warrior-band that guards the High King. He is the son of CUMHALL, murdered chief of the Fianna, killed by his rival GOLL MAC MORNA before Fionn was born. Raised in secret in the forest by TWO DRUIDESSES (Bodhmall and the Liath Luachra) so that the Morna men would not find and kill the heir, he does not know his own name for years -- he is a fair-haired boy simply called DEIMNE. T2: the young Fionn is apprenticed to an old POET named FINNEGAS who lives in a hut by the RIVER BOYNE. For SEVEN YEARS Finnegas has been trying to catch a specific fish: the SALMON OF WISDOM (an Bradan Feasa), which lives in a pool beneath the HAZEL TREES OF WISDOM at the WELL OF SEGAIS. Nine hazelnuts had fallen from the trees into the well and the salmon had eaten them; whoever ate the salmon would gain all the world's knowledge. T3: at last Finnegas catches the Salmon. In his excitement he entrusts the boy Fionn to COOK it while he prepares for the meal, warning him STRICTLY NOT TO TASTE THE FLESH -- one bite would mean all the wisdom went to the eater, not to the fisher. Fionn turns the fish on a rowan-spit over the fire. A blister rises on the salmon's skin; Fionn PRESSES IT DOWN WITH HIS THUMB to smooth the skin, and BURNS HIS THUMB on the hot juice. T4: instinctively Fionn SUCKS HIS THUMB to cool it. In that instant all the wisdom Finnegas had waited seven years for goes into the boy. When Finnegas comes back and looks at Fionn's face he sees the change and asks, 'Have you eaten of the salmon?' Fionn answers no, but confesses the burnt thumb. Finnegas replies that the salmon has chosen its own eater -- 'Take it and eat it all, Fionn, for your name is Fionn and it is you the prophecy meant.' T5: from that day forth, WHENEVER FIONN NEEDS TO KNOW ANYTHING -- who a stranger is, where a hidden enemy waits, whether a track is fresh -- he PUTS HIS THUMB IN HIS MOUTH AND SUCKS IT (or in some versions bites the thumb between his teeth) and the knowledge comes. This action is called the IMBAS FORASNAI ('great knowledge that illuminates') or later the DET FIS ('tooth of knowledge' or 'thumb of knowledge'). It is Fionn's supernatural gift for the rest of his life and the reason no enemy can ambush him. Further rungs: the NINE HAZELNUTS of wisdom motif is a Celtic mystery -- the hazel is the tree of knowledge in Irish tradition just as the apple is in the Genesis account; the WELL OF SEGAIS is the source of the Boyne in myth (real Boyne rises at Trinity Well, Newberry Hall, Co. Kildare); the pattern -- 'the intended eater is the accidental burner' -- is called the 'thumb-of-knowledge motif' in folklore studies and appears in Welsh, Norse (Sigurd tasting Fafnir's heart-blood off his finger and understanding the birds), and Finnish myth.
source: PRIMARY: Macgnimartha Finn ('The Boyhood Deeds of Fionn'), Middle Irish, preserved in Laud 610 (Bodleian) and other manuscripts, edited by Kuno Meyer (Revue Celtique 1882) and translated in Cross and Slover, Ancient Irish Tales (1936). Also in Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904) for accessible retelling. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Fionn mac Cumhaill' and 'Salmon of Wisdom' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Fionn mac Cumhaill', 'Bradan Feasa', 'Finn Eces', 'Well of Segais', 'Imbas forosnai' -- Cumhall killed by Goll, boy Fionn raised as Deimne, apprentice to Finnegas by the Boyne, seven years pursuing the salmon, nine hazelnuts from Segais, burnt thumb, sucked thumb, transfer of wisdom, Thumb-of-Knowledge. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the poet is FINNEGAS (Finn Eces) with two n's or one; whether the wisdom-motion is SUCK the thumb or BITE it (both are attested and sometimes both in the same telling).
framing_note: THE FOUNDATIONAL Fionn ladder -- every downstream Fenian topic (the Fianna, Diarmuid + Grainne, Oisin, Bran + Sceolang) leans on the T1/T2 anchor established here (§16 teach-before-test). Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (he BURNS HIS THUMB pressing a blister down on the fish he was told NOT to taste) and T4 (SUCKING his thumb to cool the burn gives him ALL of a poet's seven-years-of-fishing's wisdom in a single second). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the boy who gained wisdom by eating a salmon' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a boy at a fire on the Boyne, a great fish on a rowan-spit, a blister rising on the skin, a thumb pressed down and burnt) and let the recall be the BOY (Fionn), the FISH (Salmon of Wisdom / Bradan Feasa), the TEACHER (Finnegas), or the GIFT (thumb of knowledge / imbas forasnai). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as SIGURD tasting Fafnir's dragon-heart blood off his finger and suddenly understanding the birds' language (Norse pillar -- the DIRECT PARALLEL) or JOSEPH reading Pharaoh's dream (Christian pillar) -- a hero who gains second sight by an accidental taste. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Fenian figures (Oisin, Diarmuid, Goll -- adjacent-real from the same cycle), other wisdom-gaining scenes (Sigurd + Fafnir's blood -- Norse pillar, direct parallel; Odin drinking from Mimir's well for one eye -- Norse pillar), other magical fish (the Great Fish that swallowed Jonah -- Christian pillar), other Irish salmon (there is essentially only ONE Salmon of Wisdom). Wrong teacher: FINNEGAS the poet, not Finn's father Cumhall. Wrong river: THE BOYNE (an Bhoinn), not the Shannon.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the River Boyne as a real Irish river with its own Bru na Boinne (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth) neolithic archaeology; theology owns the STORY of the Salmon of Wisdom at the Well of Segais.

name: The Fianna: entry tests and the outsize warrior-band
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The Fianna and their initiation rites, from the Acallam na Senorach ('The Colloquy of the Ancients'), 12th c., and the Macgnimartha Finn. T1: the FIANNA are a ROVING WARRIOR-BAND of Ireland, sworn to defend the HIGH KING against foreign invaders in war and to HUNT AND FEAST in the wild during peace. In the Fenian Cycle they are led by FIONN MAC CUMHAILL; they number in the hundreds; they camp in the great forests of Ireland by season. T2: they are not the king's regular soldiers. They are OUTSIDE the ordinary social order -- they take an oath, they refuse the ordinary property and marriage rules of tuath (clan) life, and they live off the land by hunting for half the year (Beltane to Samhain) and are quartered on the king's people for the other half. Their unofficial title is 'the fian' (a war-band); the Fianna proper are the elite fian of the High King. T3: no man may join without passing the ENTRY TESTS of the Fianna, which are ferociously specific. Among them (from the Acallam and later sources): (a) BE ABLE TO RECITE TWELVE BOOKS OF POETRY from memory -- the fian is bound to the fili (poet) tradition, not merely brawn; (b) BE BURIED TO THE WAIST IN A HOLE IN THE GROUND WITH ONLY A SHIELD AND A HAZEL STICK, WHILE NINE WARRIORS THROW SPEARS AT YOU FROM NINE FURROWS AWAY -- if a single spear touches you, you fail; (c) RUN THROUGH THE FOREST PURSUED BY A WAR-BAND AT FULL SPEED, WHILE (i) not breaking a single dry stick underfoot, (ii) not letting your hair-braids come loose in the branches, (iii) not letting your weapons rattle, and (iv) leaping any thorn-bush higher than your brow and stooping under any lower than your knee without slowing. T4: the tests exclude bulk-athletes and reward speed, silence, poetry, and dignity under pressure. Any candidate who fails any single test is barred -- and no man could join whose family was still owed a blood-debt for a killing, because feuds could not be brought into the fian. T5: the tests explain a great deal about the FIGURE of Fionn -- WHY his men are all lightning-fast (Diarmuid, Caoilte the swift-footed), why they compose poems around every campfire (the entire Acallam na Senorach is Fenian survivor Oisin RECITING the old tales to St Patrick), and why the Fianna are remembered as poets AND fighters both, not one or the other. To be Fianna was to be a warrior-poet-hunter in one body. Further rungs: the twelve books of poetry are the FILI curriculum -- Ireland had an elite hereditary poetic caste and it overlaps with the fian; Caoilte mac Ronain, Fionn's cousin, is the fastest of the Fianna and the co-narrator with Oisin in the Acallam; the phrase 'as fast as one of the Fianna' remains a folk-idiom in Irish; the tests are variously described in later sources and the exact list changes -- the CORE always includes the hair-braiding-in-flight and the spear-in-the-pit.
source: PRIMARY: Acallam na Senorach ('The Colloquy of the Ancients'), 12th c., preserved in the Book of Lismore and the Laud 610 manuscript, edited by Whitley Stokes (1900) and translated by Ann Dooley and Harry Roe (Oxford World's Classics, 1999). Macgnimartha Finn ('Boyhood Deeds of Fionn'). Geoffrey Keating's Foras Feasa ar Eirinn ('History of Ireland', c.1634) preserves later Fianna-lore and the fullest list of the entry tests. Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904) for the accessible retelling. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Fianna' and 'Fenian Cycle' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Fianna', 'Fenian Cycle', 'Fionn mac Cumhaill', 'Acallam na Senorach' -- the roving warrior-band, seasonal quartering, twelve books of poetry, spear-pit test with shield and hazel, forest pursuit without breaking sticks or losing braids, poet-warrior double character, Caoilte the swift-footed. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: which entry tests are in the earliest attested Fenian sources vs Keating's 17th c. compilation (Keating collects and standardises).
framing_note: THE FOUNDATIONAL Fianna-as-institution ladder -- kids need to know these are not just Fionn's crew but a specific, ordered, poet-warrior order (§16 teach-before-test). Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (the entry tests include RECITING TWELVE BOOKS OF POETRY, and being buried WAIST-DEEP IN A PIT while NINE WARRIORS throw spears from NINE FURROWS AWAY, and RUNNING THROUGH FOREST WITHOUT BREAKING A STICK UNDERFOOT OR LOSING YOUR HAIR-BRAIDS). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Ireland's roving warrior-band' AND ask who they were; describe the SCENE (a warrior in a shoulder-deep pit with a shield and a hazel stick, or a runner threading a forest without a broken twig) and let the recall be the BAND (Fianna), the LEADER (Fionn), the SEASON (Beltane to Samhain), or the CO-CULTURE (poet-warrior). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Knights of the ROUND TABLE with their vows of chivalry (Arthurian pillar), Odin's EINHERJAR in Valhalla (Norse pillar), or the SPARTAN AGOGE (Greek pillar -- boys tested for entry into the warrior-caste). Poetry AND arms together as noble is the Irish variation kids should hear. DISTRACTOR MINE: other warrior-bands (Round Table -- Arthurian; Einherjar -- Norse; Sacred Band of Thebes -- Greek history; Merry Men -- Robin Hood pillar), other tests-of-worthiness (drawing Excalibur, sitting in the Siege Perilous -- Arthurian pillar), the FENIAN Brotherhood of 19th-c. Irish nationalism (adjacent-real but a MODERN reuse of the name). Wrong period: Fianna are seasonal (Beltane to Samhain in the wild, quartered other half), not year-round. Wrong test: the tests include POETRY, not brute-strength lifting.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the 19th-c. Fenian Brotherhood (Irish republican organisation named after these mythic Fianna) -- theology owns the LEGENDARY warrior-band itself.

name: Bran and Sceolang: Fionn's hounds who were his own cousins
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: Fionn's supernatural hunting hounds and their origin, from the Fenian tale Tochmarc Ailbe and folk-tradition preserved in the Acallam na Senorach and in Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904). T1: FIONN MAC CUMHAILL, chief of the Fianna, hunts through Ireland with a great pack of hounds -- but two are his favourites and are famous in every Fenian tale: BRAN and SCEOLANG (also spelled Sceolan, Sgeolan). They can outrun any deer, tree any boar, and understand human speech; Fionn talks to them and they answer with looks and yelps he can read. T2: Bran and Sceolang are not ordinary dogs. They are ACTUALLY FIONN'S OWN COUSINS, TRANSFORMED INTO HOUND-SHAPE WHILE STILL IN THE WOMB. T3: the story goes: Fionn's aunt (variously named -- Tuiren, Uirne, or in Lady Gregory Tuiren) marries a warrior of the Fianna; her husband's jealous JEALOUS FIRST WIFE (a woman of the SIDHE / faery folk) transforms Tuiren INTO A HOUND while Tuiren is pregnant, out of spite. Tuiren, in dog-shape, gives birth in the wild to TWO HOUND-SHAPED PUPS -- Bran and Sceolang. T4: eventually Tuiren is transformed back into a woman by Fionn's intervention on the faery-court; but the TWO PUPS remain in hound-shape and cannot be changed back, because they were CONCEIVED and BORN under the enchantment. Fionn takes them as his own -- they are family in fur -- and they hunt at his side for the rest of his life. T5: this is why Bran and Sceolang can UNDERSTAND HUMAN SPEECH (they have human minds under hound-shape), why they are so fond of Fionn (he is their cousin), and why they are treated with a dignity ordinary dogs never get in Fenian tales. When Bran eventually dies (killed, in one version, by the same enchanted stag Fionn is chasing -- Bran realises the stag is a bewitched woman and refuses to complete the kill; the enchantment breaks Bran's own life), Fionn's grief is heroic-scale, closer to a man losing a brother than a hunter losing a dog. Further rungs: the SIDHE (Old Irish 'people of the mound', 'faery folk') are the Tuatha De Danann after their retreat underground -- their transformations run through the whole Fenian cycle; the KILLED-BY-A-BEWITCHED-STAG tale for Bran's death parallels Sadhbh (Fionn's own wife) being turned into a deer, and Oisin ('little fawn') their son being born of the deer-shape; the shape-changing-of-pregnant-women motif recurs in Irish tradition and elsewhere (Cu Chulainn's mother Deichtine has a similar bird-flock encounter in some versions of the Compert).
source: PRIMARY: Acallam na Senorach (12th c., see above); Tochmarc Ailbe (Fenian tale, edited by Rudolf Thurneysen 1921); the fullest surviving narrative of Bran's birth is in Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), 'Uirne's Sons', drawing on the Fenian folk-tradition. Standish O'Grady, Silva Gadelica (1892) also preserves the tale. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Bran and Sceolang' and 'Fionn mac Cumhaill' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Bran (Irish mythology)', 'Fionn mac Cumhaill', 'Tuiren' -- the two hounds Bran and Sceolang, their aunt Tuiren transformed pregnant into a hound by a jealous faery rival, their birth in dog-shape while their mother is enchanted, their inability to be changed back, their human intelligence, Bran's death chasing a bewitched deer. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the aunt's name is TUIREN, UIRNE, or IRIRNE (three attested forms).
framing_note: The FAMOUS-HOUNDS ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (Fionn's two favourite hounds are actually HIS OWN COUSINS, born as hounds because their mother was enchanted while pregnant). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Fionn's two magical hounds' AND ask their names; describe the SCENE (a hunting pack in an Irish forest, two hounds outrunning every stag, a huntsman who talks to his dogs and they seem to understand) and let the recall be the HOUNDS (Bran + Sceolang), the KINSHIP (they are his COUSINS), or the CAUSE (their mother was transformed pregnant by a jealous rival). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as ARGUS the dog who recognises Odysseus after twenty years (Greek pillar) or GARM the hound at the gate of Hel (Norse pillar) -- named heroic dogs with story-weight. The transformation-of-pregnant-woman device is common to Celtic and Norse myth; handle it as story, no editorial. DISTRACTOR MINE: other famous mythic hounds (Cerberus at Hades -- Greek; the hound of Culann killed by Setanta -- Ulster Cycle, adjacent-real from the SISTER Irish cycle; Argus of Odysseus -- Greek pillar), other Fenian animals (Fionn's horses, Diarmuid's hunting-boar), other transformation-of-pregnant-women (Deichtine mother of Cu Chulainn -- Ulster Cycle adjacent). Wrong species: HOUNDS, not horses. Wrong cause: the mother was transformed WHILE PREGNANT, so the children were born in the shape she wore -- distinct from being turned into hounds themselves after birth.
history_overlap: None with history -- pure legend.

name: Diarmuid and Grainne: the elopement and the boar of Ben Gulbain
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The great love-tragedy of the Fenian Cycle, from Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne ('The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne'), later Fenian tale (14th-15th c. as surviving text, older in oral tradition), preserved in numerous Irish manuscripts. T1: DIARMUID UA DUIBHNE (Diarmuid O'Dyna, 'Diarmuid of the love-spot') is one of the finest young warriors of the Fianna, famous for a BEAUTY-MARK on his forehead -- placed there by a faery woman -- that makes any woman who sees it fall instantly in love with him. GRAINNE is the young and beautiful daughter of the High King CORMAC MAC AIRT; her father has betrothed her to FIONN MAC CUMHAILL, who by this point is OLD -- older than her father. T2: at the betrothal feast at Tara, Grainne looks at old white-haired Fionn and refuses the match. She looks around the hall and sees young DIARMUID with the love-spot showing under his cap. She DRUGS every man in the hall with a sleeping-potion in the drinking-cups EXCEPT Diarmuid, goes to him, and PLACES A GEIS ON HIM to elope with her -- an unbreakable magical vow he cannot refuse. T3: Diarmuid, torn between his loyalty to Fionn and the geis he cannot break, ELOPES with Grainne into the forest. For SIXTEEN YEARS Fionn pursues them across Ireland with the Fianna. Diarmuid and Grainne can never sleep TWO NIGHTS IN THE SAME BED and must move constantly. Ireland is dotted with LEABA DHIARMADA AGUS GHRAINNE ('the Beds of Diarmuid and Grainne') -- dolmens and megalithic tombs pointed out in folk tradition as where the lovers slept on their flight. T4: eventually Fionn appears to forgive them and Diarmuid returns to the Fianna. But Fionn has NOT forgotten. He organises a great BOAR-HUNT on BEN GULBAIN (Beann Ghulbain, a real mountain in County Sligo) and sends Diarmuid alone against the boar. The boar is no ordinary boar -- it is the ENCHANTED BROTHER OF DIARMUID (transformed in childhood by a druid) and a DRUIDIC PROPHECY had said the boar would kill Diarmuid. Diarmuid faces the boar and it kills him, but not before he mortally wounds it. T5: Diarmuid lies dying on the mountain. Fionn arrives. Fionn HAS THE GIFT (from the Salmon of Wisdom) that WATER CARRIED IN HIS HANDS FROM A NEARBY WELL WILL HEAL any wound. Fionn goes to the well and carries the water in his cupped hands -- but as he approaches Diarmuid, he REMEMBERS Grainne, and the WATER SLIPS THROUGH HIS FINGERS. He goes back a second time; again the water slips through. The third time he brings it -- but by then Diarmuid is dead. Grainne, when she learns, curses Fionn; the Fianna are darkened forever by this killing. Further rungs: the LEABA DIARMADA (dolmens) are real megalithic tombs still identified across Ireland by the folk-name; the LOVE-SPOT and the SIXTEEN-YEAR PURSUIT are among the most famous images in Irish folk-memory; the story is a DIRECT INSPIRATION for the Tristan and Iseult story that reached Continental Europe by the 12th c. (both feature an old king, a young queen, a young knight bound by involuntary love to elope, and pursuit -- scholars debate direction of influence).

Fenian tale, preserved in numerous Irish manuscripts (fullest text in Trinity College Dublin H.2.15 and the Book of Lismore), edited by Nessa Ni She (1967). Acallam na Senorach for the wider Fenian context. Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904) for accessible retelling. framing_note: The LOVE-TRAGEDY ladder -- one of world literature's great archetypes and the direct ancestor of Tristan & Iseult. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (Grainne DRUGS the whole royal hall and lays an unbreakable GEIS on the young Diarmuid to elope with her, at her own betrothal feast to old Fionn) and T5 (Fionn CAN heal Diarmuid with water in his hands, but LETS THE WATER SLIP THROUGH HIS FINGERS twice on purpose, and the third time it is too late). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the young warrior killed by a boar on a mountain' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a betrothal feast at Tara, sleeping-cups, a love-spot under a cap, sixteen years of flight and dolmen-beds, a hunt on a Sligo mountain, water slipping through cupped hands) and let the recall be the LOVER (Diarmuid), the QUEEN (Grainne), the MOUNTAIN (Ben Gulbain / Ben Bulben), or the WITHHELD HELP (the water Fionn let slip). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as TRISTAN AND ISEULT (Arthurian / medieval pillar -- the direct DESCENDANT, both stories the same shape and Diarmuid may have influenced it), PARIS AND HELEN (Greek pillar -- another elopement destroying an order), or DAVID AND BATHSHEBA (Christian pillar -- a king's failure to reach for a life he could have saved). Handle the LOVE-SPOT and the JEALOUSY of an old king with the same weight the tale does -- no smirking. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Fenian tragic-figures (Oisin, Caoilte -- adjacent), other tragic loves (Tristan + Iseult -- Arthurian pillar direct-descendant; Deirdre of the Sorrows -- Ulster Cycle SISTER-tragedy of forbidden love; Aengus + Caer -- Tuatha De Danann pillar), other boar-hunts (Adonis + the wild boar -- Greek pillar; Meleager + the Calydonian Boar -- Greek pillar). Wrong mountain: BEN GULBAIN (anglicised Ben Bulben) in COUNTY SLIGO, a real Irish mountain. Wrong healer: FIONN himself has the healing gift (from the Salmon), no one else.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Ben Bulben as a real Sligo mountain and the Leaba Diarmada dolmens (real megalithic tombs) as archaeological sites; theology owns the STORY of Diarmuid, Grainne, and the boar. Cross-pillar overlap: TRISTAN AND ISEULT (Arthurian / medieval) -- key different facts.

name: Oisin in Tir na nOg: Niamh of the Golden Hair and the broken saddle-girth
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The tale of Fionn's poet-son Oisin, his stay in the Land of the Young, and his fall to old age in a single moment, from Laoi Oisin ar Thir na nOg ('The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young'), composed by Michael Comyn c. 1750 from older oral tradition, preserved in numerous 18th-19th c. Irish manuscripts and printed by the Ossianic Society. T1: OISIN ('little fawn'), the SON of FIONN MAC CUMHAILL by his wife SADHBH (who had been enchanted into a deer, which is why the boy is named 'fawn' -- he is a separate ladder), is a warrior-poet of the Fianna, the finest of the fian's poets. He is Fionn's own son and the last great voice of the Fenian age. T2: one morning as the Fianna hunt on the shore of Loch Lein (in Kerry), a beautiful woman rides up out of the SEA on a WHITE HORSE. She has GOLDEN HAIR that falls to the horse's flank, wears a green mantle, and she names herself NIAMH CHINN OIR -- 'Niamh of the Golden Head', daughter of the king of TIR NA nOG, the 'LAND OF THE YOUNG'. She has come to take Oisin as her husband; she has heard his songs across the sea and loved him for them. T3: Oisin mounts behind her on the white horse; they ride WEST OVER THE WAVES; the horse's hooves never break the surface. They come to TIR NA nOG, an island in the OTHERWORLD where no one grows old, no one is sick, and the trees are always in flower and fruit at once. Oisin lives there with Niamh for what feels to him like THREE YEARS. They have children. T4: after three years Oisin grows homesick for Ireland and asks Niamh's leave to visit his father and the Fianna. Niamh warns him solemnly: he may ride the WHITE HORSE back, but IF EITHER OF HIS FEET TOUCHES IRISH SOIL, he will never return to Tir na nOg and will not survive. Oisin swears. He rides the white horse back across the waves. T5: Oisin arrives in Ireland and finds it CHANGED BEYOND RECOGNITION. Fionn is centuries dead. The Fianna are legend, not living men. THREE HUNDRED YEARS have passed in Ireland while Oisin lived his THREE in the Land of the Young. Riding through the country he sees a group of small men struggling to lift a stone. From horseback he stoops to help them; his SADDLE-GIRTH BREAKS; he falls to the ground. The moment his feet touch Irish soil, THREE HUNDRED YEARS FALL ON HIM AT ONCE -- his back bends, his hair goes white, his skin withers to parchment, his eyes go blind. The white horse gallops away riderless back over the waves. Oisin is left an ANCIENT OLD MAN blind by the roadside. In the frame-story of the Acallam na Senorach the wandering ST PATRICK finds him there, questions him for months about the old pagan days of the Fianna, and Oisin narrates the whole Fenian Cycle back to Patrick before he dies. Further rungs: the SADDLE-GIRTH breaking is the SIGNATURE image, cognate with several Otherworld-return tales where a single misstep breaks a supernatural bargain (compare Orpheus turning to look at Eurydice); the ST PATRICK frame is 12th c. Middle Irish -- placing the last Fenian survivor as the source who told the tales to Christian Ireland; the LAND OF THE YOUNG (Tir na nOg) is the most famous Otherworld in Irish tradition, cognate with Avalon in Arthurian legend (both are western island paradises where heroes go without dying); YEATS wrote The Wanderings of Oisin (1889) based on this tale.
source: PRIMARY: Laoi Oisin ar Thir na nOg ('The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young'), by Michael Comyn c. 1750, edited and translated by Brian O'Looney for the Ossianic Society (1859) -- the fullest verse narrative. Acallam na Senorach (12th c., see above) for the St Patrick frame-narrative and Oisin as last Fenian survivor. Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904) for the classic Anglo-Irish retelling. W. B. Yeats, The Wanderings of Oisin (1889) for the 19th-c. literary version. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the small men are lifting a STONE or a WOODEN PILLAR (versions vary; Comyn has stone).
framing_note: The GREATEST FAERY-OTHERWORLD tale in Irish literature. Dinner-test payoffs: T4 (Niamh's warning is FEET MUST NEVER TOUCH IRISH SOIL) and T5 (three years in the Land of the Young = THREE HUNDRED years in Ireland; a broken SADDLE-GIRTH drops him to the ground and he ages 300 YEARS IN A SECOND). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the hero who came back from fairyland and aged three centuries in a moment' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a golden-haired woman on a white horse from the sea, a ride west over waves without breaking the surface, a land where no one grows old, a broken saddle-girth on an Irish road) and let the recall be the HERO (Oisin), the WOMAN (Niamh), the OTHERWORLD (Tir na nOg / Land of the Young), or the FATAL MISHAP (the broken saddle-girth). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as ORPHEUS looking back at Eurydice and losing her at the border of Hades (Greek pillar), RIP VAN WINKLE (Washington Irving 1819, a pale descendant / American pillar borrowing this Celtic shape), or ARTHUR taken to Avalon to sleep till Britain needs him (Arthurian pillar). Time-in-the-Otherworld runs differently is a Celtic mystery kids should feel. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Fenian figures (Fionn, Diarmuid, Caoilte -- adjacent-real), other Otherworld-visitor tales (Cormac's Cup in Irish tradition, Bran's Voyage / Immram Brain, Connla's Well -- all adjacent Irish; Odysseus at Calypso's island seven years -- Greek pillar), other faery-time-tales (Rip Van Winkle -- 19th-c. American; the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus -- Christian pillar). Wrong warning: no touching IRISH SOIL, not don't-look-back (that is Orpheus). Wrong direction: WEST over the waves (Otherworld is always west in Irish tradition).
history_overlap: None with history -- pure legend. GEOGRAPHY owns Loch Lein (Killarney, County Kerry) as a real Irish lake where the tale places Niamh's arrival.

name: Fionn sleeping in the cave: the once-and-future warrior
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The folk-tradition that Fionn mac Cumhaill did not die but sleeps waiting to return, preserved in oral tradition and Fenian folk-legend from Ireland and Scottish Gaeltacht areas. T1: unlike CU CHULAINN who dies famously against a standing stone, FIONN MAC CUMHAILL in the Fenian folk-tradition DOES NOT DIE. He and the FIANNA are said to be SLEEPING in a great CAVE beneath a hill in Ireland (variously named -- some say beneath the Hill of Allen in Kildare, some say the mountain of Cnoc na Feinne, some say beneath a hill in Donegal or the Isle of Skye), waiting for the day IRELAND NEEDS THEM MOST. T2: they lie in a circle in the cave, weapons at their sides, sleeping in full armour. In the middle of the circle hangs a GREAT HORN -- the DORD FIANN, the Horn of the Fianna. IF ANYONE COMES TO THE CAVE AND SOUNDS THE HORN THREE TIMES, Fionn and the Fianna will wake, ride out, and defend Ireland one last time. T3: the legend is told of a shepherd who wandered into the cave by accident, found the sleeping warriors, and blew the horn ONCE. The Fianna stirred, half-rose on their elbows. The shepherd, terrified, DROPPED THE HORN AND RAN. As they sank back into sleep the Fianna cried out 'IS MEASA A DFHAG NA MAR A FUAIR' -- 'YOU HAVE LEFT US WORSE THAN YOU FOUND US'. If he had blown all three blasts they would have awoken fully; the one blast leaves them stirred but still bound to the sleep. T4: this SLEEPING-KING motif is one of the widest patterns in European folklore -- the same tale is told of ARTHUR at AVALON (see the Arthurian ladder), of the German Emperor FREDERICK BARBAROSSA (Charlemagne / Frederick sleeping in Kyffhauser mountain with his beard growing through the stone table), of OLGER DANSKE in Denmark, of KING WENCESLAS in Bohemia -- the once-and-future king. Fionn is the IRISH INSTANCE of this near-universal European mythic figure. T5: the folk-imagination refuses to let the hero DIE. Fionn, who spans the entire Fenian Cycle and outlives his son Oisin and his best men, is retired into the sleep rather than the grave -- a promise that the Fianna's world is not fully lost, only postponed. The tale is folk-tradition, not high manuscript: it lives in oral Irish and in the Scottish Highlands where 'Fingal' (the Scottish form of Fionn) is said to sleep beneath Ben Nevis. Further rungs: MACPHERSON'S OSSIAN (1760) -- James Macpherson's controversial 'translation' of what he claimed were 3rd-c. Scottish Gaelic poems by Ossian son of Fingal -- brought Fionn / Fingal to the attention of all Europe (Napoleon carried Ossian into battle; Goethe cited him); the Ossian was largely a Macpherson forgery, drawing on real oral Fenian tradition freely reshaped; the 'FINGAL'S CAVE' on the island of Staffa in the Inner Hebrides is named for Fingal/Fionn and inspired Mendelssohn's Hebrides Overture (1830); the ONCE-AND-FUTURE-KING trope through Arthur, Frederick, Fionn represents Europe's shared refusal to let its great heroes die.
source: PRIMARY: oral folk-tradition preserved in the Irish Folklore Commission collections (National Folklore Collection, UCD) 20th c.; Sean O'Faolain, The Great O'Neill (1942) discusses the Fionn sleeping-warrior legend; Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904) for the classical form; Douglas Hyde, Beside the Fire (1890) for late-19th-c. Irish oral versions. James Macpherson, The Poems of Ossian (1760-63) for the Ossianic/Fingal treatment. framing_note: The SLEEPING-HERO ladder -- the folklore that refuses to let Fionn die and links him to Arthur and Barbarossa. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (a horn hangs in the cave and THREE blasts must be sounded to wake the Fianna) and T3 (a shepherd blew ONCE, panicked and RAN, and the Fianna cried out YOU HAVE LEFT US WORSE THAN YOU FOUND US as they sank back). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Fionn is said to sleep beneath a hill until Ireland needs him' AND ask what awakens him; describe the SCENE (warriors in a circle in armour in a cave, a great horn hanging above them, a shepherd wandering in) and let the recall be FIONN, the HORN (Dord Fiann), the SIGNAL (three blasts), or the PARALLEL FIGURE (Arthur at Avalon, Frederick at Kyffhauser). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as ARTHUR at AVALON (Arthurian pillar -- 'rex quondam rexque futurus') or FREDERICK BARBAROSSA at Kyffhauser Mountain with his beard through the stone (Norse / Western-medieval pillar) -- honour Fionn as the Irish instance of this genuinely European trope. DISTRACTOR MINE: other sleeping heroes (Arthur -- Arthurian pillar; Barbarossa -- German-medieval; Olger Danske -- Danish; Bran the Blessed's head buried at London -- Welsh; the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus -- Christian pillar -- adjacent-real), other named Irish caves and hills (Newgrange / Bru na Boinne, Hill of Tara -- adjacent geography-real), Macpherson's Ossian (adjacent-real 18th-c. literary reception). Wrong number of blasts: THREE required, ONE was blown and it wasn't enough. Wrong wake-condition: three blasts of the HORN, not a specific bloodline or a specific king.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Fingal's Cave on the island of Staffa (Inner Hebrides) as a real basalt-column sea-cave; theology owns the LEGEND that Fingal/Fionn sleeps beneath it or that it takes his name.

name: The Giant's Causeway: Fionn, Benandonner, and the giant baby
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The Irish folk-tale explaining the Giant's Causeway on the Antrim coast, preserved in oral tradition and printed in 19th-c. folklorist collections including William Carleton and Patrick Kennedy. T1: the GIANT'S CAUSEWAY (in Irish 'Clochan an Aifir') is a REAL and famous stretch of basalt columns on the north coast of County Antrim in Northern Ireland -- forty thousand interlocking hexagonal stone columns marching down to the sea. Geologically it is a 60-million-year-old lava-flow. In folk-legend it is the work of the giant FIONN MAC CUMHAILL. T2: in the tale, FIONN (here treated as a GIANT, in the folk-tradition rather than the manuscript Fenian Cycle) has a rival: BENANDONNER, a Scottish giant living across the sea in Scotland who has been shouting insults at Fionn across the water. Fionn decides to settle it in person. He BUILDS THE CAUSEWAY -- ripping up rocks and setting them one against another across the sea from Antrim to Staffa in the Inner Hebrides (Fingal's Cave, same place-name family) -- so he can walk over dry-shod. T3: reaching the middle of the causeway Fionn catches sight of Benandonner in the distance and realises -- BENANDONNER IS FAR BIGGER THAN HE HAD THOUGHT. Bigger than Fionn himself. Fionn RUNS HOME to Ireland to think. Benandonner starts after him. T4: back home Fionn's clever WIFE (variously named -- in most versions SADHBH, Fionn's wife of the deer-tale; in others Oonagh) hides Fionn in a great CRADLE, wraps him in a BABY'S BONNET AND BLANKET, and pretends he is her infant son. When Benandonner arrives at the door, roaring for Fionn, she invites him in politely, offers him tea and griddle-bread (with iron griddles baked inside for the giant to crunch), and points to the huge 'BABY' sleeping in the cradle. T5: Benandonner stares at the enormous baby, does the math -- IF THE BABY IS THIS SIZE, THE FATHER FIONN MUST BE MONSTROUS -- and PANICS. He flees back across the causeway, TEARING UP the stones behind him as he runs so Fionn cannot follow. That is why the causeway TODAY only survives as a stump on either side of the sea -- the Antrim stretch and the matching column-clusters on Staffa in Scotland -- and the middle is broken away where Benandonner tore it up. The story explains BOTH ends of the real geological formation. Further rungs: the SAME BASALT-COLUMN formation appears on Staffa in the Hebrides (Fingal's Cave, which is 'Uamh-Binn', 'the melodious cave', in Gaelic) -- the folk-tale explains both ends of the same lava flow as remnants of one causeway; the FOLK-TALE treats Fionn as a GIANT despite the manuscript Fenian Cycle presenting him as a human-scale warrior -- this is FOLK-TRADITION drift, not high manuscript; the WIFE'S CLEVERNESS saving her giant husband is the beating heart of the tale, a domestic-scale trick winning where brute-force would have lost; the CAUSEWAY has been a tourist site since the 17th c. and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
source: PRIMARY: Irish folk-tradition preserved in Patrick Kennedy, Legendary Fictions of the Irish Celts (1866); William Carleton, Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry (1830-33); numerous later folklore-commission collections. Lady Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904). The story is oral / folkloric -- there is no medieval Fenian manuscript that contains it; it developed in the 17th-19th c. as folk-explanation for the geological formation. framing_note: The FOLK-EXPLANATION ladder for a real UNESCO-listed rock formation. Dinner-test payoffs: T4 (Fionn's wife dresses him as a GIANT BABY in a cradle so a bigger giant will think the FATHER must be even more monstrous) and T5 (Benandonner PANICS AT THE BABY and rips up the causeway as he flees -- and that is why the real basalt columns only survive at the two ends of the crossing). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the giant who built the Giant's Causeway' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a giant building a causeway of stone from Antrim toward Scotland to fight a rival, a wife hiding him as a baby in a cradle, a rival fleeing at the sight of the baby and ripping the causeway apart behind him) and let the recall be the GIANT (Fionn), the RIVAL (Benandonner), the TRICK (dressing as a baby), or the OUTCOME (torn-up causeway explains the real formation). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the CYCLOPS Polyphemus tricked by Odysseus (Greek pillar -- another giant outwitted by cleverness), Thor visiting Utgardaloki in disguise (Norse pillar -- a giant deceived by shapeshifting), or Jack and the Beanstalk (English folk-tale, adjacent). Handle Fionn AS A GIANT here (a folk-tradition variant), NOT as the human-scale Fenian warrior of the manuscripts -- state honestly if asked. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Fenian figures (the Fianna -- adjacent from manuscript tradition), other clever-wife tales, other real-geology-explained-by-myth (the Wailing Wall, Devil's Tower, the Isle of Skye's Cuillin ridges -- adjacent-real), other tricked giants (Polyphemus -- Greek; Utgard-Loki -- Norse; the Giant of the Well in Anansi tales -- African, out of pillar). WRONG NARRATIVE STATUS: this is FOLK-TALE not manuscript Fenian; Fionn as GIANT is folk-drift.
