Theology owns the folk-STORY of Fionn and Benandonner that explains the formation. This is a KEY history/geography-overlap topic -- the theology bank's angle is the STORY, geography's is the site itself.

name: Cathbad the druid and the prophecy of short life
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The chief druid of the Ulster court and his role in Cu Chulainn's story, from the Tain Bo Cuailnge boyhood-deeds inset and the Longes mac nUislenn ('The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu' -- the Deirdre of the Sorrows story), 8th-9th c. T1: CATHBAD is the CHIEF DRUID at the court of King CONCHOBAR MAC NESSA of Ulster. In the Ulster Cycle the druid is a full third of the ruling triangle -- king, warrior, druid -- and Cathbad's word is heeded by every hero from Cu Chulainn to Ferghus. He is the FATHER of Conchobar (in one tradition) and the grandfather of Cu Chulainn (in another; the genealogies twine complicatedly). T2: Cathbad runs a druidic SCHOOL at Emain Macha where he teaches the arts of divination to selected pupils. He is famous for reading the fitness of days -- what deed done on what day will bring what fate. T3: on the day the boy Setanta (Cu Chulainn) first slays Culann's hound, Cathbad is present to pronounce the naming (see the Setanta ladder). And on ANOTHER DAY, when a young Cu Chulainn (having killed the hound and become 'Cu Chulainn') overhears Cathbad TEACHING his druid-pupils that WHOEVER TAKES UP ARMS FOR THE FIRST TIME ON THIS DAY WILL WIN GLORY BEYOND ANY WARRIOR BEFORE HIM AND WILL BE FOREVER FAMOUS -- BUT WILL LIVE A SHORT LIFE -- the boy Cu Chulainn RUSHES to Conchobar and demands arms on the spot. T4: Cathbad, when he sees what has happened, DENOUNCES CONCHOBAR for arming the boy on that day of all days -- the prophecy Cathbad had spoken was true, and the boy has just SEALED HIS DOOM in a single afternoon out of eagerness. Cu Chulainn hears and answers that a LIFE WITH GLORY, HOWEVER SHORT, IS BETTER THAN A LONG LIFE WITHOUT IT. This is the CHOICE-OF-ACHILLES speech in Irish form, and it is delivered by an eight-year-old to his uncle the king. T5: Cathbad also prophesies over the newborn Deirdre in Longes mac nUislenn -- 'this child shall be the fairest woman in Ireland, but she will bring ruin on the men of Ulster, and blood, and exile' -- and Ulster's warriors demand that she be killed at birth. Conchobar refuses; keeps her in isolation to marry her himself; she elopes with the sons of Uisliu; Ulster splits; Fergus mac Roich goes into exile to Connacht and joins Medb (which is why he leads Medb's army against Ulster in the Tain). Cathbad's prophecies do not just PREDICT the future; they SHAPE it -- once spoken, every hero acts to fulfil them, thinking they are choosing freely. Further rungs: druidic PROPHECY in the Ulster Cycle is not passive; the audience of the prophecy is the mechanism by which it is fulfilled; Cathbad's role parallels TIRESIAS in Greek tradition (blind prophet whose warnings are all ignored -- Greek pillar) and MERLIN in the Arthurian (Arthurian pillar); Deirdre's story is the second-great Ulster Cycle tale after the Tain, and the Ulster warriors' banishment because of it is the reason Fergus is fighting on the Connacht side in the great war.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, boyhood-deeds inset (O'Rahilly 1976) for Cathbad's day-of-arms prophecy heard by the young Cu Chulainn. Longes mac nUislenn ('The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu'), 8th-9th c., in Lebor na hUidre, translated by Vernam Hull (1949), for Cathbad's prophecy over the newborn Deirdre and the resulting Ulster crisis. Compert Con Culainn ('The Conception of Cu Chulainn') for Cathbad's role in the birth-account. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cathbad' and 'Deirdre' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Cathbad', 'Deirdre', 'Conchobar mac Nessa', 'Longes mac nUislenn' -- Cathbad as chief druid at Emain Macha, day-of-arms prophecy overheard by the boy Cu Chulainn, short-life-lasting-fame trade, prophecy over Deirdre and the ruin she brings on Ulster, banishment of the sons of Uisliu, Fergus going into exile. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Cathbad's day-of-arms prophecy is heard directly by the boy Cu Chulainn or reported (in Recension I the boy overhears while Cathbad is teaching pupils outside).
framing_note: The DRUIDIC-PROPHECY ladder -- explains WHY Cu Chulainn's short life is a choice, not just a fate, and connects the Tain to the Deirdre tragedy. Dinner-test payoffs: T3 (Cu Chulainn OVERHEARS the prophecy and RUSHES to arm himself, deliberately choosing the short life for glory) and T5 (Cathbad's prophecy over the newborn DEIRDRE causes Fergus's exile and is the reason Fergus leads the Connacht army against his own Ulster people in the Tain). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the chief druid of Ulster who prophesied Cu Chulainn's short life' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a druid teaching his pupils outside a fort, a boy overhearing the fate-of-the-day, an infant girl foreseen to ruin a kingdom) and let the recall be the DRUID (Cathbad), the CHOICE (short life + glory), or the CURSED CHILD (Deirdre). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as TIRESIAS the blind prophet whose warnings Odysseus and Oedipus ignore (Greek pillar), MERLIN foreseeing Camlann and unable to prevent it (Arthurian pillar), or the PROPHETS OF ISRAEL announcing dooms that come true precisely because they were announced (Christian pillar). Prophecy that shapes what it predicts is a mythic mystery -- honour it. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Ulster Cycle druids (there is really only Cathbad as chief), other prophets (Tiresias -- Greek; Merlin -- Arthurian; Cassandra -- Greek), other Ulster figures (Conchobar the king, Fergus in exile -- adjacent-real from same cycle). Wrong role: Cathbad is the DRUID / PROPHET, not the king or the warrior. Wrong prophecy: 'short life + lasting fame' is the day-of-arms prophecy for CU CHULAINN; the 'ruin on Ulster' is the DEIRDRE prophecy -- two different prophecies from the same druid.
history_overlap: None with history -- Cathbad is a purely literary druid figure.

name: Emer and the wooing: Cu Chulainn's wife who out-witted him first
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The wife of Cu Chulainn and the wooing-test that sends him to Scathach, from Tochmarc Emire ('The Wooing of Emer'), 8th-9th c., Rawlinson B 512 manuscript. T1: EMER is the daughter of FORGALL MANACH ('Forgall the Wily'), a chieftain of Lusk in what is now north County Dublin. She is FAMED throughout Ulster for the SIX GIFTS of a woman: BEAUTY, VOICE, WISDOM, SEWING, EMBROIDERY, and CHASTITY. Cu Chulainn, as a young man, hears of her and rides to Lusk to woo her. T2: at the ramparts of Forgall's fort Cu Chulainn finds Emer working at embroidery among the noblewomen. They begin a courtship IN RIDDLES -- Cu Chulainn speaks in cryptic imagery about his journey; Emer answers in equally cryptic imagery about her father's defences and her own free will. The passage of exchanged riddles (called the ROSC of Emer) is one of the most sophisticated dialogues in early Irish literature and shows Emer as MORE VERBALLY DEXTEROUS than Cu Chulainn -- she can spar with him mind-to-mind before body-to-body. T3: FORGALL, when he hears of the suit, does not want Cu Chulainn (or ANY Ulster warrior) as a son-in-law. He goes DISGUISED to Emain Macha and, pretending to be a Gaulish visitor, tells Cu Chulainn that a warrior of his promise is INCOMPLETE without training abroad and should study with the great warrior-woman SCATHACH on the Isle of Shadow. His plan is that Cu Chulainn will die on the perilous journey and never return. T4: Cu Chulainn DOES go to Scathach -- Forgall's ruse succeeds in sending him -- and there Cu Chulainn completes the training that will make him unbeatable (see the Scathach ladder). But he returns ALIVE. He storms Forgall's fort at Lusk, KILLS FORGALL (who dies falling from his own rampart), takes Emer, and marries her. T5: Emer is the ONLY WOMAN CU CHULAINN LOVES; she is his partner through the whole cycle, waiting at DUN DEALGAN (Dundalk) while he defends the ford, receiving the report of his death, and eventually dying HERSELF OF GRIEF on his grave. In Serglige Con Culainn ('The Wasting-Sickness of Cu Chulainn'), when Cu Chulainn falls in love with the fairy woman Fand, it is EMER who confronts Fand at the meeting, argues her out of taking Cu Chulainn away, and forgives her husband. Emer's grief-death at Cu Chulainn's grave is one of the earliest attested love-deaths in European literature. Further rungs: EMER'S SIX GIFTS is a famous formula still cited; the RIDDLE-DIALOGUE with Cu Chulainn ('what is the road you have travelled?' and so on) is written in a difficult archaic Old Irish that is one of the oldest surviving passages of Irish literature; Cu Chulainn had OTHER women (Fand the fairy, Aife the warrior-queen who bore Connla, the wife of Uath perhaps) but EMER is the wife.
source: PRIMARY: Tochmarc Emire ('The Wooing of Emer'), 8th-9th c., preserved in Rawlinson B 512 and other manuscripts, translated by Kuno Meyer (Archaeological Review 1888) and A. G. van Hamel (Compert Con Culainn and Other Stories, 1933). Serglige Con Culainn ('The Wasting-Sickness of Cu Chulainn') for Emer's confrontation with Fand. Aided Con Culainn for Emer's grief-death. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Emer' and 'Cu Chulainn' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Emer', 'Tochmarc Emire', 'Forgall Monach', 'Serglige Con Culainn' -- Emer's six gifts, the riddle-dialogue with Cu Chulainn, Forgall's disguise sending Cu Chulainn to Scathach as a trap, storming of Lusk, Emer's confrontation of Fand, Emer's death on Cu Chulainn's grave. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact list of Emer's six gifts (sources sometimes number them differently).
framing_note: The WIFE ladder. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (Emer OUT-RIDDLES Cu Chulainn in courtship -- her mind beats his mind before any of the sword-work) and T3 (Emer's own FATHER Forgall DISGUISES himself and TRICKS Cu Chulainn into going to Scathach hoping he'll die on the way). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Cu Chulainn's wife of the six gifts' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a young hero at a rampart, women at embroidery, a courtship conducted in cryptic riddles, a jealous father in disguise) and let the recall be the WIFE (Emer), the FATHER (Forgall Manach), or the SIX GIFTS. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as PENELOPE keeping the suitors off with her loom (Greek pillar), SIF the wife of Thor (Norse pillar), or MARY of Bethany choosing the better part (Christian pillar). Emer as CO-INTELLIGENT partner not passive wife is the Irish variation to honour. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Cu Chulainn women (Fand the fairy from Serglige Con Culainn, Aife the warrior-queen who bore Connla -- both adjacent-real from same cycle), other clever wives (Penelope -- Greek), other Ulster women (Deirdre -- Ulster Cycle, adjacent). Wrong father: FORGALL MANACH ('the Wily'), not King Conchobar. Wrong fate: Cu Chulainn DOES go to Scathach and DOES return alive; the trap fails.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Lusk (Lusca in Old Irish) as a real north-Dublin place; theology owns the STORY of Emer's home there.

name: The Morrigan: war-goddess in three shapes
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The Ulster Cycle war-goddess who haunts Cu Chulainn, from the Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I (O'Rahilly 1976) and Aided Con Culainn. T1: THE MORRIGAN ('the Great Queen' or 'the Phantom Queen') is a WAR-GODDESS of Irish mythology -- a shapechanging figure who appears on battlefields in the form of a WOMAN, a CROW, an EEL, a WOLF, or a HORSE, and by her presence turns the tide of the fighting. She is one of a triad of war-goddesses (with Macha and Nemain, or sometimes Badb) but is the most independently active. T2: in the Tain the Morrigan comes to CU CHULAINN in her most beautiful WOMAN-SHAPE as he is defending the fords. She offers him her love and her help in the coming war. Cu Chulainn REFUSES her -- he cannot afford distraction, he does not know she is a goddess, and he says so bluntly. The Morrigan turns cold: 'if you will not have my love, you shall have my hate.' T3: three times in the following fights the Morrigan interferes with Cu Chulainn in the middle of single combat. She appears as a WHITE HEIFER charging his enemy's cattle-herd across the ford to distract him; as an EEL wrapping around his feet in the water; as a GREY-RED SHE-WOLF driving other cattle at him. Each time Cu Chulainn wounds her -- he crushes the eel with a heel-stamp, breaks the heifer's leg with a slingshot, blinds the wolf's eye with a stone. He does not know he is fighting the goddess. T4: after each fight the Morrigan appears elsewhere as an OLD WOMAN MILKING A COW with the identical wounds -- lame in one leg, blind in one eye, one arm crushed. She offers Cu Chulainn milk in each visit; he accepts, blesses her, and thereby (unknowingly) HEALS the wounds he inflicted. Only at the last visit does he recognise her, and she rides away laughing. The Morrigan cannot be his enemy after those blessings, but she cannot forget the refusal either. T5: on the DAY OF CU CHULAINN'S DEATH, when he is tied to the standing stone Clochafarmore mortally wounded, the Morrigan comes at last as a RAVEN and lands on his shoulder to drink his blood. This is the SIGN that confirms his death to the enemies waiting at a distance (see the Death ladder). The war-goddess he refused as a lover comes to him at last as the announcement of the corpse. Their relationship is one of the most complex hero-and-goddess relationships in myth. Further rungs: the Morrigan is part of the TUATHA DE DANANN (the older Irish gods) -- she is present at the second Battle of Moytura in the Cath Maige Tuired against the Fomorians; the modern D&D word 'MORRIGAN' comes from her; scholars distinguish MORRIGU (singular) from na MORRIGNA (the three-fold form including Macha and Badb); Badb is the CROW-form specifically, sometimes distinguished from the Morrigan.
source: PRIMARY: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I, edited by Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976), the Morrigan's offer to Cu Chulainn at the ford and the eel/heifer/wolf interference sequence. Aided Con Culainn for the raven on Cu Chulainn's shoulder. Cath Maige Tuired ('The Battle of Moytura'), 9th-10th c., for her role in the wider Tuatha De Danann context. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'The Morrigan' and 'Badb' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'The Morrigan', 'Badb', 'Macha', 'Nemain' -- war-goddess in three shapes, offer of love to Cu Chulainn and his refusal, eel-heifer-wolf interference, milked cow woman with identical wounds healed by unknowing blessing, raven on the shoulder confirming death. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the Morrigan comes as EEL / HEIFER / WOLF specifically or in slightly varied triads (Recension I is the anchor; later versions vary).
framing_note: The WAR-GODDESS ladder. Dinner-test payoffs: T2 (the goddess OFFERS HER LOVE to Cu Chulainn on the battlefield and he BLUNTLY REFUSES) and T4 (Cu Chulainn WOUNDS her three times in animal-shape without knowing, then HEALS her three times unknowingly by accepting milk from an old cow-woman). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the shape-shifting Irish war-goddess who took a raven's form' AND ask her name; describe the SCENE (a beautiful woman at a ford making an offer, animals appearing in the water and on the flank, a old milking-cow-woman with mirroring wounds, a raven landing on a corpse) and let the recall be the GODDESS (Morrigan), her SHAPES (raven / eel / heifer / wolf), or her ROLE (war-goddess). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as HERA turning against Achilles for a slight (Greek pillar), the VALKYRIES choosing the slain (Norse pillar), or the ANGEL OF DEATH in the Christian tradition (Christian pillar) -- female supernatural figures who bring the fate of the battlefield. DO NOT sanitise the sexuality or the violence; the Tain does not. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Irish war-goddesses (Macha and Badb are her SISTERS, sometimes conflated; Nemain is a related figure), other Cu Chulainn interlocutors (Cathbad the druid, Scathach the teacher, Emer the wife -- all adjacent-real), other shape-changing goddesses (Hera as heifer -- Greek pillar; Freyja with the falcon-cloak -- Norse pillar), other war-related raven-figures (Odin's ravens Huginn and Muninn -- Norse pillar). Wrong triad: the MORRIGAN + MACHA + BADB (the Morrigna), sometimes with Nemain added -- three or four depending on source. Wrong death-form: RAVEN on the shoulder, not eagle, not vulture.
history_overlap: None with history -- pure mythology.

name: Cu Chulainn kills his own son: Connla at the water
strand: Western myth: Cuchulainn (Ulster Cycle) + Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna (Fenian Cycle)
scope: The Aided Aenfhir Aife ('The Death of Aife's Only Son'), Ulster Cycle tragedy, 8th-9th c., preserved in Yellow Book of Lecan and other manuscripts. T1: while training with SCATHACH on the ISLE OF SHADOW (see the Scathach ladder), CU CHULAINN defeats the rival warrior-queen AIFE in single combat, spares her life, and lies with her for one night; she conceives a son. Before Cu Chulainn returns to Ireland he gives Aife three commandments to pass to the child: (1) that the boy shall come to Ireland when he is seven; (2) that he shall NEVER TURN BACK from any warrior he meets on the road; (3) that he shall NEVER TELL HIS NAME to anyone who challenges him. Cu Chulainn also leaves Aife a GOLD RING to be given to the boy when his finger fits it, so that Cu Chulainn will recognise him. T2: seven years later a small boy sails alone into the harbour at BAILE's STRAND on the Ulster coast. He is doing bronze feats with a slingshot on the beach -- stunning seabirds without killing them and bringing them back alive. The Ulstermen at the fort send warriors down to challenge him. Because of the SECOND commandment the boy will not turn back; because of the THIRD he will not give his name. He is polite and cheerful and refuses. T3: one after another the Ulster champions go down against the boy. Conall Cernach (Ulster's second-greatest warrior) fights him and is BEATEN by a child. Word comes to Cu Chulainn at Dun Dealgan. Cu Chulainn goes down to the strand himself. His wife EMER pleads with him NOT to go -- she has heard the story and suspects who the boy is -- but Cu Chulainn goes. T4: father and son meet on the beach without knowing each other. Cu Chulainn asks the boy's name; the boy refuses (as his mother taught him). They fight. Cu Chulainn cannot best the boy in ordinary combat -- the boy has the same feats Cu Chulainn learned from Scathach, because his mother Aife trained him. Cu Chulainn, driven to it, calls for the GAE BOLG. He hurls it from his foot in the sea (the same technique that killed Ferdiad) and the barbed spear goes into the boy's belly. T5: the boy falls; Cu Chulainn cradles him. As the child is dying he takes off his GOLD RING and gives it to Cu Chulainn -- 'I am CONNLA, son of Aife. This is the token my mother sent.' Cu Chulainn, holding his dying son, cries out that had he lived, all Ulster would have knelt to him. He carries the body up to the assembled Ulstermen and LAMENTS -- 'I HAVE KILLED MY OWN SON FOR THE HONOUR OF ULSTER.' The three commandments Cu Chulainn HIMSELF laid on the child -- meant to make Connla into a great warrior -- have killed him. Further rungs: the Aided Aenfhir Aife is a DIRECT parallel to the Persian tale of RUSTAM AND SOHRAB (the Shahnameh) and the Germanic HILDEBRANDSLIED -- father unknowingly killing warrior son -- so exact in the pattern that scholars debate common Indo-European origin; the boy's HUMANE MISSILE-USE (stunning birds without killing them) marks him as morally superior to the warriors who go down against him; the story is one of the most emotionally overwhelming pieces of early Irish literature.
source: PRIMARY: Aided Aenfhir Aife ('The Death of Aife's Only Son'), 8th-9th c., preserved in Yellow Book of Lecan and other manuscripts, edited by A. G. van Hamel (Compert Con Culainn and Other Stories, 1933) and translated by Kuno Meyer. Tochmarc Emire for the earlier Aife episode. Thomas Kinsella, The Tain (Oxford, 1969, appendix). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Connla' and 'Aided Aenfhir Aife' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Connla', 'Aife', 'Cu Chulainn', 'Aided Aenfhir Aife' -- three commandments left by Cu Chulainn for the unborn son, gold ring token, seven-year-old boy landing at Baile's Strand, stunning birds without killing, Ulster champions defeated one by one, father-son combat, Gae Bolg killing the boy, dying recognition. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the boy is CONNLA (Old Irish Conlaech) or CONLA -- both spellings attested; the strand is BAILE'S STRAND (Traigh Bhaile, the modern Dundalk bay area).
framing_note: The most tragic single tale in the Ulster Cycle. Dinner-test payoffs: T1 (Cu Chulainn HIMSELF laid the three commandments -- never turn back, never give name -- meant to make his son a great warrior, but those commandments are what SEALED THE DEATH) and T4/T5 (father kills son with the GAE BOLG on the beach, and only when the boy dies does the GOLD RING TOKEN reveal who he was). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the hero who killed his own son on the beach' AND ask his name; describe the SCENE (a child sailing alone into a harbour and doing sling-feats, Ulster warriors falling one by one to a boy, a father called from Dun Dealgan, a Gae Bolg cast in the surf, a dying child pulling a gold ring off his finger) and let the recall be the FATHER (Cu Chulainn), the SON (Connla), the MOTHER (Aife), the RECOGNITION TOKEN (gold ring), or the FATAL WEAPON (Gae Bolg). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as RUSTAM killing SOHRAB in the Shahnameh (Persian -- direct parallel, but out of pillar; do NOT use as distractor because non-Western), HILDEBRAND unknowingly fighting his son HADUBRAND in the Hildebrandslied (Norse-Germanic pillar -- direct parallel, may use), or David hearing 'ABSALOM my son my son ABSALOM would God I had died for thee' (Christian pillar) -- a father-son death that undoes a hero. Grade-10 kids can handle it; the tragedy is the point. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Cu Chulainn deaths-caused (Ferdiad the foster-brother -- adjacent from the same cycle), other father-son unknowing-combats (HILDEBRAND + HADUBRAND -- adjacent-real from Norse pillar; Oedipus killing his father Laius is REVERSE-direction -- Greek pillar), other Ulster women (Emer his wife, Deirdre, the Morrigan -- adjacent). Wrong father: CU CHULAINN, not Conchobar or Ferghus. Wrong son: CONNLA / CONLAECH by AIFE (the Scottish warrior-queen), not by Emer. Wrong weapon: the GAE BOLG kicked from the foot -- the same weapon that killed Ferdiad, and the boy is Cu Chulainn's OWN SON.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Baile's Strand (Traigh Bhaile, in the Dundalk bay area) as a real Louth beach; theology owns the STORY of the father-son combat there. Cross-pillar: HILDEBRANDSLIED (Norse-Germanic) parallels the tale exactly -- theology-bank material both, key different facts.
